maintopic: RESIGNATION FROM THE CABINET OF HON. MR. PATENAUDE.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to state, in. the absence of the Prime Minister, that Mr. Patenaude has tendered his resignation, and that the correspondence in reference thereto will be laid .on the table of the House as soon as the assent of the Governor General has been obtained.
On the Orders of the Day:
I desire to lay on the table of the - House an Order in Council passed on the 8th of June, 1917, constituting a controller of fuel for the Dominion of Canada.
Who is the controller?

Mr. C. A.
Magrath. The order in Council is as follows:
The Committee of the Privy Cunoil have had- before them a report dated 8th June, 1917, from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, submitting the following observations on the coal situation in Canada:-
Last winter' very considerable difficulty and hardship were experienced owing to shortage of supplies and congestion of transport, resulting in increased prices to consumers, serious temporary curtailment of production in factories, and much discomfort and privation in the homes of the poorer classes in towns and cities. These causes bid fair to continue and with increasing force during the present season, and are added to by the scarcity of labour for the mines, the increasing difficulties in transport and the added demand for coal in both the United States and Canada owing to the ever increasing exigencies of the war.
At the present moment the outlook for the coming season gives cause for grave anxiety and calls for prompt and efficient action if subsequent shortage and its consequent privations are to be avoided. The Quebec district, which formerly drew for its needs for railways and factories some 2,000,000 tons of bituminous coal from Nova Scotia mines, cannot estimate on more than 2'00,00'0 tons from that source. Nearly all the prospective output of these mines will be required for local needs, bunkering purposes and the use of the Intercolonial Railway. This transfers the supply of this deficiency to the United States mines, whilst in Middle Canada the demands have to be met, if at all, by drawing upon United States sources.
Here two difficulties are encountered. First, the high price and shortage of supply in the United States mines, caused by extraordinary demands and reduced .output owing to scarcity of labour. The entrance of the United States into the war and the vast preparations necessary 'for the equipment of sea and land forces and the growing needs of the Allies call for vastly increased output of coal and added restraint of export for other than war purposes. In the second place transport by land and water is daily becoming more inadequate compared to the increasing volume of freights to be moved, and freight costs are continually increasing.
In the westerp prairie provinces the supply has been diminished by strikes in some of the mines and in respect to those working the output is restricted by the tendency to neglect putting in orders during the summer season, and consequent failure to haul coal to consuming centres during the slack and favourable season.
The minister represents that it seems, therefore, to be necessary that a competent fuel controller should be appointed:
1.	To examine into the coal situation of eastern and middle Canada from the Atlantic coast to the Rockies.
(a)	As to the probable demands for consumption therein for the coming season.
(b)	As to the output of Canadian coal that can be relied upon towards meeting those demands and what, if any, measures can be adopted to increase this output.
(c)	As to the sources outside of Canada [DOT] from which the deficiency can be provided, and the possibility of obtaining the necessary amount.
(d)	As to the possibility of providing sufficient transport for the carriage of both Canadian and foreign coal from the points of production to distributing points.
(e)	As to the possibility of early and continuous co-operation between producers, carriers and consumers, with a view to economizing and facilitating the needed supply.
2.	That in the course of and in connection with such investigation, he be authorized to confer with and co-ordinate the different interests with a view to ensure so far as possible a sufficient supply of coal for Canadian

requirements during the approaching autumn and winter seasons and from time to time to report and recommend to the Government ways and means for effecting the same.
The minister recommends that Charles A, Magrath be appointed Fuel Controller and be charged with carrying out the purposes outlined in the foregoing memorandum, and that all expenses incurred by him for clerical assistance and travelling and living expenses in connection therewith constitute a charge upon and be paid from the War Appropriation Funds.
The committee concur in the foregoing and submit the same for approval.
OSgd.) Rodolphe Boudreau, Clerk of the Privy Council.

speechtext:
No. The Orders in Council are as follows:
at the government house at

Monday the 11th day of June, 1917.
Present:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council.
Whereas, by reason of war conditions, it is considered necessary to provide means whereby the grain of Canada in excess of domestic requirements may be made available for purchase by or on behalf of His Majesty's Government of the United Kingdom and of the Allied Powers, and that the distribution of domestic requirements be controlled in such manner and under such conditions as will prevent to the utmost possible extent any undue inflation or depreciation of values by speculation, by the hoarding grain supplies, or by any other means;
Therefor His Excellency the Governor General in Council, under and by virtue of the provisions of the War Measures Act, 1911, is pleased to make the following regulations and the same are hereby mode and enacted accordingly :-
1.	The Governor General in Council may appoint a Board to he designated "The Board of Grain Supervisors of Canada" hereinafter called the Board. Such Board shall be honorary and shall consist of not more than twelve (12) members.
2.	The Members of the Board shall be paid travelling and living expenses while actually engaged in the duties of the Board but otherwise shall receive no renumeration.
3.	The Board shall make such inquiries and investigations as from time to time it deems necessary to ascertain what supplies of grain ore no.v available or will be available. The Board shall ascertain the location and ownership of such grain and what transportation end elevator facilities are available in connection therewith, as well as all conditions connected with the marketing and the market price of the same. For the purpose of any inquiry or investigation held by the Board, the Board and the several members thereof shall have all the power of a commissioner acting under part 1 of the Enquiries Act.
4.	The Board shall have power from time to time to fix the price at which grain stored in any elevator may he purchased, and the conditions as to price, destination or otherwise under which grain may he removed from such elevator and may also prescribe what grain shall be sold to millers or milling firms in Canada or elsewhere (hereinafter called "Millers") and what grain shall be sent to the United Kingdom and the Allied powers and it shall be the duty of the Board to issue such orders and take such action as it

deems necessary to facilitate at all times the transportation and delivery of grain in excess of domestic requirements to the United Kingdom and the Allied powers.
(*a) Any price so fixed shall be subject to the approval of the Chairman of the Board.
(b) The Board may from time to time appoint an executive committee of not less than three of its members of whom the Chairman shall be one and may assign to such executive committee any duties or powers within the competence of the Board.
5.	The Board shall have power to receive offers for the purchase of grain from millers and from the Wheat Export Company Limited, or from any other person or body corporate, hereinafter referred to as "Overseas Purchasers" representing or acting for the Government of the United Kingdom or for any of the Allied nations or for any combination of the same, and from time to time to fix the prices at which such grain shall be sold.
6. The Board shall have power to take possession of and sell and deliver to millers or to overseas purchasers at the prices so fixed grain stored in any elevator, and to account and pay over to the owners thereof the proceeds of such sales after deducting all expenses connected with the taking possession, sale and delivery.
7.	The Board shall, as far as possible, and having regard to position and the cost of transportation, fix a uniform price throughout Canada for grain of the same kind quality and grade.
8.	Notwithstanding anything in the Grain Act or in the Railway Act, the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada shall have power to order any railway company to provide cars and other transportation facilities for handling grain and to transport as directed, grain taken possession of or owned by the Board.
9.	Every person shall truthfully and promptly answer any inquiry made by the Board or by any person duly authorized on its behalf about any matter within its powers or duties, whether such inquiry is made verbally, in writing, by telegraph, or in any other way.
10.	In this order "Elevator" means and includes any terminal, country, private, public and hospital elevator, and any elevator licensed by the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada.
11.	The Board, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may make any regulations it deem§j£iecessary for the purpose of fully and effectively carrying out the objects and provisions of these regulations, and in particular, but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations.
(a)	For appointing representatives in different places in Canada for the purpose, from time to time, of making known in such localities the prices for grain fixed and other regulations or directions made by the Board, and for reporting to the Board any violations or any order issued by the Board or any regulations made hereunder, and generally for assisting the Board in the effective discharge of its duties;
(b)	To authorise the engaging of clerks, employees and asistants and the paying of their salaries;
(c)	Creating offences and providing penalties in respect of violations of any order made
143£
by the Board or of any regulation made hereunder.
(Signed) Rodolphe Boudreau.

On motion of Sir Thomas White, the House went into Committee on Bill No. 68, to amend the Civil Service Act.
On section 2-persons placed in third class undeT 1908 Act who had passed qualifying examination, etc., eligible for promotion to second class:
Might I ask if a distinction is drawn between those who have passed the examination and those who have not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section applies to those who had prior to the coming into force of the Civil Service Act of 1908 passed the qualifying examination, ot have been appointed under sections 37 or 40 of the Civil Service Act, chapter sixteen of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906: that is to say, this section applies to those who have passed the qualifying examination or have been appointed on account of technical skill or special training under the provisions of sections 37 and 40 of the former Civil Service Act.
Under the present section are those who did not pass such an examination wholly ineligible, or is machinery provided whereby they may become eligible for promotion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only way in which they -could become eligible is by qualifying under the present Civil Service Act of 1908, or by being specially mentioned in the Estimates. In this Act we deal only with those who have passed the qualifying examination, or were otherwise qualified under the legislation in effect before the Civil Service Act of 1908 came into force.

Is any provision made for the -comparatively large number of officials who were not required to be qualified before the coming into force of the Act?
SiT THOMAS WHITE:	My hon. friend
will observe that this section refers not only to those who have passed the qualifying examination, but also to those appointed under sections 37 and 40 of the Civil Service Act, by reason of technical knowledge or some special skill which they possessed.

I have received a number of communications the substance of which I might give for the benefit of the minister. One of the officials suggests that the annual increase of from $50 to $100 might also apply to those employees who have been at the maximum of subdivision B of the Second Division for not less than three years. This amendment would not in any way interfere with the existing minimum and maximum salaries of the Second Division, but would have the effect of promoting these employees into subdivision A of the Second Division.	'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We gave that matter very special consideration and came to the conclusion that as we were giving special advantages to the Third Division by increasing the maximum to $1,300, that would be sufficient to meet the case. For instance, any one in the Third Division who

has attained the maximum of $1,200 may now go up to $1,300. If he merited it, he would receive the annual statutory increase until that figure was reached. Then, if he passed the Civil Service examination, he would be eligible for appointment to the Second Division.

Those who complain are those who have reached the maximum of $1,600 and have been at that figure for some years. Nothing is done for them, and they ask that they should be promoted to subdivision A of the Second Division. Some men have been at the maximum of $1,600 for four or five years, while the cost of living has been going up all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend must be talking about the Second Division.
Yes, the man who is getting $1,600.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He would have to. wait until he was promoted. He is eligible for promotion to Subdivision A without passing an examination. It is a question for the departmental head to consider in each case. The civil servant is not debarred from advancement by inability to take the examination, because when he advances to the Second Division no further examinations are necessary.

Sir George Murray in his report recommended that the Third Division should be divided into three subdivisions, but no effect is given to that recommendation. I thought it my duty to bring these matters to the attention of the minister. I am probably better known to some of the officials than are many other members, and I suppose that is why I have been asked to make these representations on their behalf. These people find that they have remained without promotion for seven or eight years, and that, notwithstanding' the increased cost of living, nothing whatever 'has been done for them. Though they have reached the maximum of their class, and may have been at that point for four or five years or more, they get an increase of only $100, and, unless promoted by departmental action, they get nothing more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This legislation
is merely to- exempt an official from taking the examination. It has nothing to do with giving him promotion. Whether he is promoted or not would depend upon his ability, and uppn his chief recognizing that ability. We are dealing, in this section,
only with those who qualified for the service prior to 1908, but have not qualified for promotion under the existing legislation.

I am sure that the hon. minister does not wish to do injustice to any civil servant, but there have been cases in which civil servants have been recommended for promotion by the chief of the branch, and that recommendation has been set aside by higher authority. There is another point to Which I might call attention while I am on the subject. Under the law a civil servant, after he has been a certain number of years in the service, may be superannuated. But, as to the time when he shall be superannuated he is not given a hearing, nor has he any appeal. One of the oldest employees of the House of Commons, one who, when I was Speaker, was one of the ablest of the staff, learned on the street one day, after forty years of service, that he had been superannuated, though his fellow-members of the staff knew that he was just as competent for his duties then as he had been at any time before. I understand that under the rules of the Indian 'Civil Service, a civil servant who is superannuated has the right to appeal. A provision of that kind, if introduced into our law, would, apply no matter which party happened to be in power. I think that a man who has been a long time in the service should have a protection of that kind. The minister should consider whether this would not be a fair amendment to make.

Section agreed to.
On section 3:
3.	Sections twenty-nine and thirty land subsection one of section thirty-two of the said Act are repealed, and the following are substituted therefor:-
"29. In the second division, the minimum and maximum salaries shall be as follows:
In subdivision A, $1,600 to $2,100;
In subdivision B, $1,000 to $1,600.
"30. In the third division the minimum and maximum salaries shall be as follows:
In subdivision A, $1,000 to $1,300;
In subdivision B, $600 to $1,000.
"32. (1) The minimum and miaximum salaries for the positions of messenger, porter, sorter and packer, and for such other positions in the lower grades as are determined by the Governor in Council, shall be $600 and $1,000 respectively, and, unless the official record to be kept as hereinafter provided shows him to be undeserving thereof, there may be given to every person holding such a position an annual increase of fifty dollars until the maximum is reached."

I would urge the minister to consider paying higher salaries to those civil servants who are in the Third Division.

If salaries from $1,600 to $2,100 are paid to those in the Second Division on the ground that the amount is needed for the support of their families, I do not see why the man who belongs to the Third Division, and who may have the same family responsibilities, should be paid so little. In view of the high cost of living, I do not see why those in/ Subdivision A of the Third Division should not be paid from $1,000 to $1,500, and those in Subdivision B from $600 to $1,200, with an increase of $100 a year in either case. I am told that those in the Third Division sometimes have qualifications equal with those in the Second Division, and are even doing work of equal importance. If there are any men who need increases in order to support their families certainly they must be those who now are lowest in the Civil Service. A salary of $600, or $700, or $800 for a man-I do not say for a woman, because I am against high salaries for women, though there are many in this House who disagree with me on that point, but I still believe that the salaries paid to women should not increase beyond a certain amount-any such salary for a man with a family to support is certainly not enough. I think the minister should be willing to increase the salaries to the figures I have stated, and I believe that *such an amendment of the Bill should appeal to the sense-of fairness of honourable members of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boulay) will observe that we are fixing the minimum and maximum of the grades. There is nothing to prevent a promotion from Subdivision B to Subdivision A, provided the necessary recommendation is made and agreed to by the minister and the Government. Sir George Murray recommended that the Third Division should be divided into three subdivisions. But here there are only two. In all offices it is customary to have the junior clerks and those who do the less skilled work paid at a less figure than those who are trained and who do more expert work. That is the reason for the subdivision of the division into A and B, with the differences in scale as shown in the Bill.
It is to be pointed out that we get in the service every year a number of untrained, or practically untrained, young women, or maybe young men, who are not really worth more than $500 or $600 a year tp begin with. If they went into a financial or commercial office outside of the Civil Service, they would not receive more than that amount to start with, in fact, in financial offices, 
they start young clerks at a less ampunt than $600 per annum. Nevertheless, on account of the conditions which have prevailed, especially since the outbreak of the war, we have thought that we should give an increase especially in the lower grades of the service, that is to say, in the third division, and we have raised the minimum from $500 tp $600 in that division and also in respect to messengers, packers and sorters. But, we have gone farther than that. We have provided that every one in these two classes may be granted an. increase for the present fiscal year of $100; that is to say a messenger or clerk in the Third Division who is now getting $500 a year would be advanced to $600 a year, which is the minimum in each of the classes now, and in addition he would receive this year $100, if worthy of it, and the statutory increase as well. In some cases there will be an advance from $500 for the fiscal year to $750, which is a very substantial increase, being fifty per cent over the amount at present paid. I am inclined to think that the measure deals fairly and justly with the situation which my hon. friend has in view, namely, the high cost of living and its bearing upon the salaries especially of the lower grades up to $1,000. We were more interested in these than in those above $1,000 because the pinch comes in respect to the lower grades. On the whole, I am hopeful that this will meet the conditions that exist to-day fairly satisfactorily.

Why not put it up to
$1,200? I see no reason why, because every member of this House knows that under conditions which are prevailing to-day, it is impossible for a man tp support a family on less than $1,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend suggest that instead of the minimum of $600 we should fix the minimum at $1,000.

No, it would be all right to start at $600 but you should increase it by $100 a year and the increase should be made statutpry and not subject to the recommendation of the deputy minister or the chief of a branch because sometimes the poor fellows may not get it at all. Then, as it is now, they would only increase at the rate of $50 a year. If they had the ex-pectatipn of being able to go to $1,200, it would encourage them to stay in the service and perform their duties faithfully. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance said that those in the Third Division were not as highly qualified as those in the

Second Division. If I am not mistaken men require to be well qualified before they are admitted to the Third Division. I see by an examination paper .set for admission to the third division that some very hard questions are put and it requires considerable ability to pass the examination for admission to this division. Those who are admitted are pretty well qualified to do any kind of work in the department. It may be that, with regard to some kinds of work, they may require a certain amount of practice and instruction before they become proficient, but on the whole they must have more than ordinary qualifications to secure admission to this division. I think it would be nothing but fair to hold out to them the hope that they might go to $1,200 by increases of $100 yearly without reference to the recommendation of the deputy head or head of the branch. If they are subjected to this condition there may be half of them left aside each year, if t'he chief of the branch does not want them increased but they will have to support their families and live just the same as those who have been fortunate enough to secure an increase in their salaries.

My hon. friend from
Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has stated very clearly the case for the lower grades in the Inside Service and I can only second his remarks. As regards the salaries of $500 or $600 paid to messengers in the Inside Service, I would appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) to seriously consider the position of these men. I have received a batch of letters from mostly all the messengers in Ottawa and I believe they present a fair case. Really, with the cost of living as it is in Ottawa to-day, a man having a family of two or three children cannot possibly face the conditions of life. I have here some figures which were published in one of the papers of this city as to the increase in the cost of living showing how the family budget has soared within the past four years. This statement is based on statistics collected by the Department of Labour and it is based on the average prices in about sixty cities in Canada. In April, 1914, the family budget was $7.51 per week while in April of this year it had risen to $10.77 and with the addition of coal, wood, lighting and rent, the total reached $17.34 per week. The price of commodities has soared to that figure. Everybody in this House knows that. Therefore, as His Majesty's Government must be carried on, the Government,
without being unduly generous, should at least be fairly liberal. I am not one of those who say that because a man is in the Civil Service, having chosen to enter it, he should receive privileged treatment. But, as you are carrying on His Majesty's Government, it is only natural to expect that you will deal fairly and generously with the employees of the Government. With reference to this question of the salaries in the Inside Service, I appeal on behalf of the man who is at the foot of the ladder; I am not speaking for those in. the higher grades; they can well take care of themselves. Some years ago my hon. friend the Minister of Finance introduced, or promised to introduce, a Bill to deal with the Civil Service and I told him that he should not confine himself to the Inside Service but that he .should have some regard to the Outside Service. The host of Government employees who have congregated in the city of Ottawa and who are employed in the large public buildings should not alone be considered. You have in every city, town and hamlet of the Dominion faithful employees of His Majesty's Government. I must give due credit to the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) for, in his recent interview with representatives of labour, promising to deal generously with the employees of his department in the Outside Service and I think he has dealt with them quite generously and liberally. I also approve of his action in promising that he would give preference to returned soldiers.
I take the Post Office Department because I am more familiaT with that department than with any other. The misfortune of the Post Office Department .since 1911 has been that its principal officer, the Postmaster General, has been so often changed that the poor sorters and the poor railway mail clerks have been completely forgotten. Let us hope that in the near future there will be more permanency in. that department, and that its employees will be looked after in a proper way. I again appeal to my hon. friend, and I say to him that he should not confine his efforts to deal fairly with the Civil Service to the Inside Service only, but should extend those efforts, to the Outside Civil Service.
Let me read the petition which undoubtedly was sent to other members of the House by the railway mail clerks who have been clamouring for the last five or six years for an increase of salary. This memorial was sent to my hon. friend the ex-

Secretary of State, the Hon. Mr. Patenaude. It was addressed to him ae Postmaster General, as he was simply locum tenens in the Post Office Department. It is dated April 25 and is as follows:
"Hon. E. L. Patenaude,
Postmaster General, Ottawa.
Honourable Sir,-
- At your request, we are here representative of the Railway Mail Clerks operating railway postal routes east of Sudbury, nine divisions, totalling (approximately eight hundred clerks, to lay before you our claims to have the Provisional Allowance, an allowance long enjoyed by our western brethren, extended to the clerks of the eastern divisions.
The necessity of immediate assistance is indeed pressing, owing to the fact that living conditions have increased so much in the past few years, so much thiat we who are of fixed salaries find them inadequate to support us in comfort, indeed if present conditions continue living will fast become burdensome. All wage-earners in commercial life have had their salaries (adjusted from time to time to meet these conditions. In proof I will quote you a few necessities taken from the February issue of the Labour Gazette, published by the Department of Labour for the provinces of Eastern Canada. Food stuffs have increased since 1910 51 per cent., light and fuel 21 per cent., clothing 80 per cent., hotels and restaurants 75 per cent.
We feel th(at in asking for the Provisional Allowance we are not asking for an increase in salary. The clerks of the western divisions have enjoyed this allowance for over thirty years, owing to the excess cost of living over the east. Conditions have changed in the past few years, until at the present time living conditions are on a parity throughout the Dominion.
We feel that we are now $300 behind our brother clerks of the Post Office staff. In 1914 a Bill passed the Commons and Senate raising the Post Office Clerks' annual increment from $50 to $100, after $800 had been reached. A similar Bill unanimously passed the Commons granting Railway Mail Clerks the same consideration. This Bill, unfortunately for us, was rejected by the Senate owing to its being connected with legislation of a contentious nature. The same standard of education is required to enter either branch of the service and it is beyond our powers to imagine why we, who labour longer and under more trying circumstances, are expected to perform our daily duties for so much less remuneration.
In view of these several facts we respectfully ask that the Provisional Allowance of $15 per month be extended to the Railway Mail Clerks who are not at the present time enjoying this consideration; that Bill No. 147 of May 4th, 1914, to amend the Post Office Act be re-introduced and that it be made retroactive ; namely that the annual increase to Railway Mail Clerks be $100 instead of $50, and that the maximum salary be made $1,600. This last clause to be added to the Bill in order that all clerks be benefited.
We have the honour to be, Sir,
Tour obedient servants,
The Committee."
This is the case as presented foy the railway mail clerks. They ask, first, that the 
provisional allowance which is granted to the railway clerks in the western divisions 'be made applicable also to the eastern di-visione, and I think that they are absolutely justified in this request. Second, they ask that the Bill giving them a better emolument, which was introduced in 1914, and which was withdrawn because it was connected with something of a contentious nature to which the Senate objected, be reenacted, with a further suggestion that a clause be added giving a maximum .salary of $1,600. The railway mail clerks of Canada perform a most valuable and a most dangerous duty, and as a result of the danger connected' with their constant travels from one end of the country to the other during the cold weather of winter, their health is more often impaired than that of the every day officer in any department. The medical men in the House will bear ime^ out in the statement that they are obliged to carry insurance policies, which, of course, everybody should have.
At a higher premium.

Of course, yes. For those considerations, I plead with the Minister of Finance to kindly consider the case of the railway mail clerks. Not only the railway mail clerks, but the clerks in the Post Office, the sorters, the letter carriers and the postmasters in the country, are deserving of further consideration. The additional work which is imposed on the mail carriers on account of the extension of rural mail delivery system should also be taken into consideration. I know that this means -an additional expenditure, and I generally plead for a reduction- in expenditure; but there is a noble expenditure, there is a necessary expenditure, it is expenditure which affects His Majesty's servants. I again ask my hon. friend to enlarge the scope of his Bill and not to restrict it to the Civil Service at Ottawa.
It is a mistake to think that the whole Civil Service is centered here in Ottawa. The 'Civil Service extends from one end of the country to the other, and I daresay that the outside civil servant in the distant hamlet, or vilage of Canada, is obliged to know more and has to take more responsibility than the man in Ottawa who has at hi-s disposal the advice, the experience, the wisdom of his superior officers. In view of the higher cost of living-let me repeat those figures, they are startling, but they are not less true. Foodstuffs have increased since 1910 by 51 per cent; light and fuel, 21 per cent; clothing, 80 -per cent; hotels and

restaurants, 75 per cent, surely the Government ought to take into consideration these facts and figures, and act accordingly.

I am pleased indeed
to express my concurrence in. the sentiments utteied by the hen. member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux). There is no doubt that at the present time the high cost of living should in fairness be taken into consideration fixing the salaries of those in the Civil Service.
While the farmer has been paying more since the war started for many of the things which are absolutely necessary to the carrying on of his business, he is getting more for his produce. The wage-earner and the labourer have plenty of work at higher wages than formerly. The persons who get no relief are those who receive fixed salaries. Food costs them more than it did before, and they have no other means of providing for their needs than the fixed salary. Consideration should be given to that class of the community. Ottawa is not the only place where foodstuffs are higher than they were before the war, nor is it the only place where men and women are engaged in the Civil Service. I should be the last to say that no consideration should be given to the civil servants in Ottawa. But, applying my remarks to both sides of the House, I think that the reason why more consideration has been and is being given to the Inside Service at Ottawa than to civil servants outside is because several thousand of them in Ottawa have votes and exercise their franchise when elections come on. On the other hand, in a given constituency elsewhere in the Dominion, practically only a few persons who exercise the franchise are engaged in the Civil Service. In all fairness, more consideration should be given to men in the Civil Service, outside of Ottawa.
My hon. friend has referred to the couriers and the country postmasters. Since the inauguration of parcel post, the work of the country postmaster has enormously increased, while his remuneration has not increased proportionately. The burden bears still more heavily upon the couriers, who sign contracts for four years. Four years ago there was no parcel post system. Many of those who had been carrying mail had made a considerable amount of money by carrying parcels at 5, 10 and 15 cents 'each. In this way they added to their salaries; and no doubt they took that into consideration when they made their tender. Then the system of parcel post
was inaugurated, and the couriers are now obliged to carry a much larger number of parcels without any added remuneration. In many cases they have been obliged to use a heavier or larger rig than they formerly used, perhaps using two horses instead of one, thus adding to the expense of carrying on their work without the compensation of increased remuneration. This is absolutely unfair. I brought the matter to the attention of Hon. Mr. Pelletier when he was Postmaster General, and he agreed [DOT]that prevailing conditions were unfair to the couriers and to the country postmasters. The late Hon. Mr. Casgrain also agreed with me in that respect. Nothing, however, has been done in the matter.
I think that more consideration should be given to the railway mail clerks also; I thoroughly agree with what the member for Rouville has said in that regard. The duties of these officials require them
4 p.m. to work during long hours.
Their occupation is considered by the insurance companies to be more or less dangerous, and if they take out insurance they have to pay an extra premium because of the extra risk. These men are not getting the consideration from this Government that they should receive in the matter of their salaries.
The hon. gentleman to my right (Mr. Boulay) has made some remarks with regard to the clerks in the Third Division. Any third class clerk has the right to fit himself for a position in the Second Division. I do not agree with all that my hon. friend has said in regard to these clerks. Opportunities for the advancement of young men and women in our country are plentiful; they need not enter the Civil Service unless they wish. It is in the interest of Canada that men and women who enter the service should take pains thoroughly to qualify themselves for the duties which they are called upon to perform in that service. I am glad that a number of university graduates are entering the service; I would like to see more of them in it. Persons who enter the Third Division should be sufficiently ambitious to fit themselves for the examination of the Second Division and qualify for a higher salary. For this reason I have no fault to find with the salaries set forth in the Bill which apply to this class of the service.
Let me again ask the Government to take into consideration the salaries paid to civil servants outside of Ottawa, and to the claims of the couriers on rural mail routes and of the country postmasters.

As one who was unfortunate enough to spend three or four years in the outside Civil Service, I wish to associate myself with the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me in asking that the Government give favourable consideration to any requests in the matter of remuneration made by members of the outside Civil Service. I do not say a word against increases in the inside service; I am quite sure that they are well merited, and if I made any suggestion at all it, would be that the increases should be greater.
I should like to say a word or two on behalf of the railway mail clerks and of the railway mail service generally. Railway mail clerks carry on a very hazardous work, taking their lives in their hands every day. Their pay is not at all commensurate with the work that they perform. They have to have the knowledge of a postmaster; they have to rely entirely upon themselves, having, as the member for Rouville has pointed out, no superior officer from whom they may obtain direction or assistance. I am not in agreement with certain action taken by a former Postmaster General in connection with the qualifications of railway mail clerks. Under the old order of things, a man had to pass a qualifying examination before receiving his permanent appointment. Hon. Mr. Pelletier changed that, and provided that by passing the preliminary examination a man could be permanently appointed to the railway mail service. He would then get his increases up to $1,000, where he would stop until he passed the qualifying examination.
I cannot understand by what process of reasoning one can come to the conclusion that after a man has spent so many years of his life in learning work of that kind, he should stop at the thousand dollar stage until he has learned again many of the things that he forgot after he left the public school.
The hon. member for Frontenac also mentioned the mail carriers, and I would like to say a word or two in their behalf. The whole system of paying mail carriers is wrong, and I would not permit contracts of that kind to be let on tender at all, because there are many cases where a man could be saved from his own foolishness in tenderihg too low. In any constituency in Canada where the Government throws open a small mail contract for local competition, for some reason or another, many people think that a dollar secured from the Gov-

ernment is worth five dollars from any one else, and they will tender far below a reasonable rate. After they receive a contract, the trouble for the member starts; he is immediately deluged with petitions and requests for more remuneration, but unfortunately the law of the land does not permit the Government to give them that. The mail service of Canada should be standardized and so much per mile allowed according to the nature of the country to be travelled-I am speaking now of land travel per mile-so that every man would know, when he started, how much he was going to receive. In that way he would not be subjected to unreasonable competition by some one who might wish to put in a tender for work about which he knows nothing.	. ,
. I also wish to say a word on behalf of a branch of the Railway Mail Service, known as the transfer class. I do not know whether this matter has been brought to the attention of the minister or not, but there is a class of men working in the transfer business at salaries that are a disgrace to this country. Any one going to Toronto between six and eleven o'clock at night will find officers of the Post Office Department hauling heavy trucks of mail from one train to another, working like slaves, for a salary of .$2 a day. No man can possibly live on such a wage, and it is the duty of the Government, as a matter of ordinary humanity, apart altogether from the question of common sense, to see that that branch receive a reasonable wage.

On several occasions
deputations of mail carriers in Montreal have waited on me at my residence and have laid before me their grievances and copies of petitions sent to the minister in charge of that department pleading for an increase in salary. The case of the mail carriers, of the hardships they are suffering and of the>
faithful service they give, are well known to every hon. member. In this instance the petition which I received was similar to the one which was forwarded by their confreres in. the city of Toronto with whom they were working in harmony. I promised these men I would say a word in their favour, and I have done so now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is not the only action which the Government is taking or purposes taking with reference to the Civil Service. I explained the other day that this, was an amendment to the Civil Service Act which relates to the In-

side Service at Ottawa, which, for some reason, comes so far as salaries are concerned under the supervision of my department. Take the case of contracts referred to by the hon. members for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) and for North York (Mr. J. A. M. Armstrong). Those can. be dealt with without any change in the existing legislation if, in the estimation of the minister, it is proper for them to be dealt with, and most of the cases which have been drawn to our attention this afternoon in connection with the Outside Service can be dealt with without any change in existing legislation. When the Bill was before the House recently I stated that in the Supplementary Estimates provision would be made for whatever increases were regarded as necessary by the ministers of the several departments in connection with the Outside Service. I drew to the attention of the House that to-day, without any further legislation the Minister of Customs, to take one case, can and does frequently recommend to the Treasury Board an increase of fifty dollars or $100 per year in the case of officials in his department outside of the city of Ottawa, that is to say, in the Outside Service. It is similarly proper for the Postmaster General to provide in his Estimates a lump sum which would he available for the purpose of granting certain increases in his department in the Outside Service. Similarly with regard tG the Outside Service of the Department of Inland Revenue, and also with regard to the Outside Service of the Department of the Interior or the Department of Public Works. All that this legislation does is to amend the Civil Service Act relating to the Inside Service. As I say, it is not the only action which the Government has taken, is taking or purposes taking with respect to the Service as a whole. The reason why I am not attempting to deal with all those is because legislation is not necessary for the most part, and because they are under the jurisdiction of other .ministers. Many of the observations which have been made this afternoon, and which, of course, are quite relevant to the discussion of this Bill-I find no fault m that regard-might be made more usefully when the Estimates of the ministers in question (are under consideration in this House. Then the ministers who are immediately connected will have the views of the members and can take in their Supplementary Esti-imates su.ch action as may be necessary to meet the situation drawn to their attention.

Although, as the Minister
of Finance has stated, that probably another time than the present would be more opportune for discussing this matter, I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without mentioning one class of civil servants with whom I am particularly well' acquainted. I [DOT]refer to the officers of the border at Fort Erie, Bridgeburg, and Niagara Falls. The salaries that those men are receiving are a disgrace. The immigration officers on the trains, a splendid class of fellows, who put in long hours, intelligent civil servants and good citizens, are working on a salary of 5800 to $850 a year and maintaining their families at the places I have mentioned, (where the cost of living is probably higher than in any other part of Canada. I think in the Immigration Department the salary of $800 or $850 a year is permanent without iany increase, and these -men with the present high cost of living and high rent are having a hard task in trying to maintain their families, and they should receive more money. I am glad the Minister of Customs is in his seat, and I trust ihe may remember the officers, of his department at the boundary line. I believe there is a general feeling on both sides of the House that these civil servants should receive higher salaries than they are receiving at the present time. We hear talk of coalition in Canada at this time. This is a case on which we should have coalition; we should .all agree that there be no criticism in future as to increased expenditure for salaries in the departments, and that we .should give these men higher salaries in order that they may live in comfoTt.
Mr. VERViILLE: Every one admits that it is necessary that salaries should be increased because the cost of living is increasing. It matters very little how much you give a man to live on; the question is how much he- can buy with that money. The Minister of Finance .should take .steps to check the present increase in the cost of living, and then perhaps the salaries he may give some of the officials will be worth while. Otherwise, in two or three months from now those increases that he may grant will make no difference to the recipients, because the rise in prices will be greater than the increase in salary. The remedy, I believe, lies in preventing an increase in the cost of living, and I would ask the minister to look at that end of the line as well as increasing the salaries. He should certainly take into account the high cost of

*Jiving when providing for the salary increases.

There is considerable
anxiety on the part of a number of employees of the Inside Service relative to subsection 30. It will not benefit, for instance, those who have not passed any qualifying examination, and it appears there are quite a number of employees in this class. Perhaps the minister would make a statement clearing the matter up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated some time ago in reply to my hon. friend fron) Bona-venture that the maximum of the Third Division has been increased by $100. Any employee in that class, if thought worthy of an increase, can go up to $1,300 by annual increases of $50.
Even if he has not passed any qualifying examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, provided he is in that division. In this Act we are not exempting from qualification those who had not passed a qualifying examination previous to the Act of 1908, or were not otherwise qualified under the legislation of that day. We have thought it proper, however, to exenapt from the necessity of taking an academic examination those who were qualified under the Civil Service Act of 1908. We did not feel warranted in going further than that. If there are any in the Third Division who were in that division prior to the coming into force of the present Act, and who have not passed the qualifying examination or were not otherwise qualified under the legislation of that day, the only way in which they can qualify for promotion to the Second Division is by taking the examination provided for under the existing Civil Service Act, or by being specially named in the Estimates. I could imagine a situation-I have no particular case in view-in which it might be impossible for some excellent clerk to pass the examination qualifying him for the Second Division, and where it might be proper for the minister to name him in the Estimates; in. other words, to place him in the Second Division by naming him. In that case clerk would not have to pass an academic examination. Objections might perhaps be urged to that course. I have no particular case in mind, but it seems to me there might possibly be cases in which this might fairly be done.

I have no doubt the minister is aware that a number of returhed soldiers are greatly concerned as to the exact position they would occupy in the 	,
service if they were taken into it. Would a returned soldier who had previously been in the Civil Service, and who had been on active service at the front for two years, be put at the minimum of his class?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking from memory, I think he would be subject to the present Civil Service Act; there may be an Order in Council relating to the matter, 'but I do not recall it at the present time. Of course, it would be open to the minister to name such an official at a certain salary, but I do not see how the soldier could be exempt from the provisions of the Civil Service Act relating to entrance to the service, unless he was specially named. If the returned soldier were qualified to enter the [DOT]Second Division he could enter it, of course; but if he was not qualified I should say that he would start at the minimum provided by the existing legislation. I am not quite positive about that, because some Orders in 'Council have been passed relating to returned soldiers, but that is my opinion offhand.

There is a feeling among the returned soldiers that the men who have been-on active service at the front for two years should be allowed the yearly increase given to the men at home. For instance, if a soldier had spent two years at the front and in the ordinary course of events would have received a yearly increase of $50, he should he on the same footing with those who have remained at home and should be given an increase of $100.

I am in sympathy with practically everything that has been said in connection with this Bill. As I understand it, though there may be members of the Outside Service in the city of Ottawa, the bulk of the Outside Service are outside of this city.
There are outside civil servants in the city of Ottawa; for instance, officers in the Post Office and the Customs Departments.

Yes, but when speaking of the Outside Service we are thinking more of those outside the city of Ottawa. It was of these employees that the hon. member for Frontenac was speaking, when he said, whether rightly or wrongly, that not so many votes were affected. Personally, I think the Outside Service outside the city of Ottawa should receive a little more attention than the Outside or Inside Service in the city of Ottawa. I have been going around the different departments for a good

*many years, and what I am going to say does not apply merely to this Government, because I was a member of the House for a long time during the late Administration. There is no doubt in my mind that the Inside Service at Ottawa is over-manned. There are undoubtedly men and women clerks in the different departments at Ottawa who are overworked and have to return to the office in the evening; they are not being paid the salary they should receive. I have always taken the ground that any man who works, whether he be labourer or clerk, should receive good wages; that has been a principle with me in my own business. But I do think that this matter of getting into the different departments in the city of Ottawa is overdone. There are boys and girls here who are in the service rather for recreation and to have a little pocket money-and in saying that I think I know exactly what I am talking about. Now, I want it clearly understood that I am not including in my remarks any one who is necessary to the efficiency of the service, but it is a very nice thing to be in the service and get your pay every month. I am confident that if there were a weeding out of those who watch for five o'clock to come, there would be quite a reduction in the Inside Service here.
Now, I wish to refer to the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid). He is a good fellow. In my constituency I have about six or seven customs officers. We have to have them. They get $800 a year. Nearly every one of them has no other source of income and is expected to live on that $800. It is impossible; it cannot be done. Yet I have been very unsuccessful in my applications to the Minister of Customs to have the salaries of these men increased. They should be increased. It may ibe said that in some cases these officers are not necessary. That may be true in some towns; but when there are only six customs officers in a constituency as large as mine, I do not think the service can be said to be overmanned. These men have been paid $800 a year as long as I have known anything about it, and there has been no change in spite of the increased cost of living.
Now, I wish to say a word about the carriers of the rural mail. In Ontario and Quebec, and also I presume, in the Maritime Provinces, mral mail has been a success.	I am a great advocate of the 'rural mail system. What we are trying to do as representatives of the people is to make the country a place in which people will wish to dwell.
We have been talking for many years about " back to the farm," and I am a great believer in that doctrine; the farm is a good place, and it is our duty to make the farm as attractive as possible. There are several things that have aided very much in making country life more attractive. One is the telephone, and another is the rural mail. People to-day, especially in these stirring times, are intensely interested in getting a daily paper and in getting the mail. But what has been my experience in trying to establish rural mail routes? I have established very few. Why? The farmers are quite willing to supply the boxes-that is a matter of about $4 each and it is about all they are asked to supply. Then comes the question of carrying the mail, and when it comes to that I find myself up against the real thing. I cannot get men to take that position-and that is remarkable enough, when you think of it; you can't get men to take a Government job.
Even with tenders?

With tenders, or without tenders. I do not know the exact figure, but there is a certain percentage given to the carriers in the western provinces in addition to what is paid in the provinces that are more thickly settled. But I cannot get men to carry the mail throughout the country; and that is why there are in my constituency so few rural mail routes. Some one suggested to-day what I thought was a good idea, that this should not be by tender, but that a proper scale should be fixed. In eastern Canada your dwellings are more along certain lines and are close together, but where, as in my constituency, you have men living on a half-section or a quarter-section, the rural mail delivery is more difficult.
So, there are two classes of men in my constituency to whom the Government is not paying living wages to-day; one class is made up of the customs officers, and the other of the man carrying the rural mail. I do not know whether this is the right time under the rules for this discussion, but it is a good time for me to get in my kick about these people. I want the Government to take these men into consideration and give them what they deserve.

My attention has been called to what appears to be an injustice under this measure to a certain class in the Third Division. The committee is aware that the object of the legislation is to improve the situation of those in the lower

grades, and to give them a living wage. When the Bill was under consideration the other day, I was under the impression, and I think the committee was also, that the majority in the Third Division would be benefited by section 3. But the benefits of that section are confined entirely to those who have passed the qualifying examination before 1908. I am astonished to find that there are 450 men in the Third Division who were not called upon to pass the qualifying examination, and who will be outside the scope of this Bill. They have been in their several departments for nine years or more, and are just as well qualified for departmental work as those who have passed the qualifying examination. It seems to me we ought to make all the men in the Third Division who are certified to by the deputy minister eligible for advancement to the Second Division, and not confine it to those who had passed the qualifying examination. Otherwise these men, many of whom are married, will be left without any redress under the provisions of the Bill. There is a further class in the Third Division to which I wish to refer. Under section 4 of the Bill any person in receipt of a salary of less than $1,000 may be given an increase of $100 in order to bring him up to $1,000. I am told that there are 392 men in the Third Division who will not benefit by this provision, because they are receiving between $1,000 and $1,200. It does seem to me that less than $1,200 a year for these men, ninety per cent of whom are married, is absolutely inadequate for their livelihood under present conditions.
I would like to have this section include men who are in receipt of salaries up to $1,200, thus giving them the additional $100 from 1st April last. These are two objections to the Bill brought to my notice which I think, are worthy of being brought to the attention' of the committee before the Bill is passed.

I have no desire that any civil servant in Ottawa should receive less than a living wage. I have had reason to ascertain the exact number in the service of the Crown in Ottawa, and I findi that that number is nearly 12,000, and the aggregate annual pay nearly $12,000,000.
I have no hesitation in saying that the service here could be reduced by ten per cent and be much more efficient that it is now. This saving of a million and a half a year to this country, which is now paid to those who render no efficeint service to 
the state, would produce results, I think, that are very much to be * desired.
There are not only too many civil servants in the employ of the Crown in Ottawa but there are too1 many inefficient civil servants in the employ of the Crown. There are too many efficient civil servants in the employ of the Crown outside of Ottawa who are being insufficiently paid. In the city in which I live, and I am not accustomed to taking that as an example, but it illustrates the conditions that prevail in Vestern Canada; I found last year a graduate of Queen's University, a woman who had graduated in Arts with honours who was in the service-of the Crown receiving the magnificent sum of $55 per month in one of the public departments. There are many men and women in western Canada -receiving $50, $55, $60 or $70 per month. I had a letter to-day from a letter carrier who, with his wife and family, is endeavouring to keep the wolf from the door on the magnificent sum of $65 a month. I had another communication yesterday morning from a soldier who has returned from the present war wounded and who is now in the. service of the Crown receiving $75 per month and supporting himself, his wife and family. On every occasion on which I bring these matters to the attention of the responsible ministers, they always point out that we are in the midst of a war, that the Minister of Finance, who is very much burdened with the necessity of providing money to carry on this war,- cannot provide money to meet the demands-the reasonable demands-of the servants of the Crown. If you can find money to inciease the pay of the 12,000 civil servants in the city of Ottawa-all of whom will not receive increases of pay-but if you can find money to pay them a living wage, then I submit that the people who are out in the country living under circumstances much more difficult, where it is more expensive, must be heard and their case must be dealt with. This is what I submit to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. If he can find money for those who are included in this measure,
I submit that he can find money for the servants employed in the Department of the Interior. If he can find more money to be paid to the members of the Inside Service who are being dealt with here, he can find money to pay the servants in the Department of Customs and the Post Office Department throughout the country and the money can be found by taking the Civil Service in this city, putting it upon an effi-

cient basis, which means that it can be cut down ten per cent, thereby increasing its efficiency and proficiency, and the money thus saved can be used to pay a living wage to those who are working for $50 and $55 per month. That is my opinion and it sets forth what I believe to be the duty	of	the	Government	at thismoment.	I know	of nothing	that isso much calculated to bring the Government into disrepute, to make for bitterness and strife, to create a feeling of animosity against constituted authority and the creation	of	those	socialistic	tendencies that	are	manifesting themselves in
[DOT]the state in an alarming manner, than the absolutely inadequate salaries that are being paid to the servants of the Crown outside [DOT]of this city. I say that after a careful study [DOT]of t'he situation and what I have learned [DOT]in relation to Calgary applies with equal force to other places. I see my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) in his place now. I was in Edmonton not long since and a number of gentlemen connected with the service of the letter carriers and mail clerks spoke to me and asked me if I would lend my influence, such as it was, in support of my hon. friend from Edomonton in an effort to increase the pay of these men. That is the position as I understood it.
Further, it is my view that in the West we have a peculiar grievance in relation to [DOT]the pay of the members of the Civil Service. The cost of living, according to the [DOT]statement which my hon. friend from Rou-[DOT]ville (Mr. Lemieux) read, has increased [DOT]fifty per cent over what it was a few years ago. In the West there is an increase of [DOT]more than that, and no man with a wife and family in these times can pay rent, pay for the cost of food, educate 'his children and decently clothe them on $55 a month. He cannot do it; it is impossible to do it, and I do ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who has brought in this Bill that affects only the Civil Service in Ottawa, to remember those less fortunate servants of the Crown who are serving in the capacity of clerks in the custom house, mail .sorters or letter carriers, or servants of the Crown in great departments like the Department of the Interior, or in outside work, as some of them are, carrying the mails in country districts, and in country post offices. I would further remind him that after all a living wage for every man and woman who serves the State is, in the judgment of those who have formed an opinion from a caTeful investigation of the subject, one of the surest and best indications of a really advanced state. There can be no decent civilization in the state if men and women are struggling to keep body and soul together, not knowing where the next day's meal is coming from while thinking for the whole people at only $50 or $60 a month. It is impossible. Think of that young lady who gave four years of her life to acquiring an academic education and taking honours at Queen's University working in the Department of the Interior at Calgary for $55 a month. Under these circumstances what inducement is there for anybody to get an education in the State?
It is perfectly absurd.
Another essential is I think that men and women should be treated on an equality in relation to the pay they get, having regard to the service they render. A difficulty that is often met with is that the pay is based on the number of years of service without any regard whatever to efficiency. I find that a man, having worked twelve years in the service, gets a salary that is based upon annual increases, while the man who is giving twice as much service to the State is getting only $600 or $700. There must te payment of salaries on the basis of real merit and work. What commercial institution keeps a man in its employ and pays him a salary because he has been so many years in its service without regard to his work or to what he is worth to that institution? Nobody does that. Would my hon. friend the Minister of Finance when he was manager of the National Trust Company, keep a clerk in his employ, pay him $1,000 a year and increase his pay annually by $50 or $100 altogether regardless of his efficiency while another man who had come into the service and who was of equal ability would only get $700 or $800? I cannot believe that he would. Then, it should not be done in Ottawa any more than in any other place. My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) quite properly pointed out the reason why. It is important, even in times of war, that we should take stock of the situation, and taking stock of the situation the Minister of Finance and his colleagues should discuss the whole matter, make an adequate survey of the situation and determine the number of men and women that might be dropped from the service because they are inefficient. That is suggestion number one. If he determines how he can cut down the number of people who are working for the Crown because .of inefficiency, he can then determine to what extent he can increase.

the salaries of those who remain having regard to their efficiency and the work they are doing.
I want to tell this House something that was done in this country during the last six months. In a great department in the public service men and women were working together. They were all being paid the same amount-$60 per month. The head of the department said: "I am not satisfied that these people are all worth the same money; therefore, I propose to establish a merit system and I will fix, first of all, what I regard as the minimum amount of work and then I will provide that at the end of the month for an increase in the salaries of my employees based upon the measure of work they have done during the month and the accuracy with which they have done it. Well, the result was that two or three of the employees are still getting the minimum pay but the most of them stimulated by the desire to increase their pay, have shown such proficiency that they are now getting as much as $10 per month more than they were getting at the start. Why cannot that be done in the public service? How do railways deal with their men? They do not pay two men the same salary because they may be working at a particular job. They deal with them on the basis of merit, and I do this afternoon ask the Minister of Finance and his colleagues once more to remember the men and women who live outside of Ottawa and who find themselves dependent upon the salary or wage that the father earns, a wage which is wholly inadequate at this time to keep body and soul together and to clothe the children so that they may attend school in town, village, hamlet or remote country. This state even in war can do nothing better to show that, after all, our every day civilization is in keeping with that for which our men are striving overseas, than by seeing that those who serve the state in a civil capacity are paid a reasonable wage for the work they render to the State, and which, in its way, although not as important, is just as essential as the military service given by our men overseas.
I have listened carefully to the remarks that have been made, and I do not want to annoy the Minister of Finance by my remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Go ahead, I am glad to hear you.

Of course this may not
be exactly the right time to talk about the Outside Service because later there may be some provision, as the minister explained, for that class of employees. I concur in the remarks of those who have spoken in favour of that class. It is certain that they are not paid salaries commensurate with the present high cost of living. I wish particularly to insist upon better treatment of those who are in the lower grades of the Inside Servidh, particularly the Third Division, , subdivision B. I am not of the opinion of my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) when he says it is very easy for a man of that class to qualify and pass from the Third Division to the Second Division after a certain number of years. I have been all my life a very good scholar, and I think he has been also, yet he would be in great trouble to pass an examination of that kind, and I also-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-and go into the Second Class of the Civil Service. When a man has been in the Third Class of the Civil Service and is over thirty years of age, he is in no position to go to work and pursue a new course of study to fit himself for the qualifying examination. So if a man is to spend all his life in Subdivision B of the Third Class I feel that the Government should see its way ' clear to give him a sufficient wage to enable him to support himself and his family. I know men in Ottawa, married men, who are getting $650 a year, and surely they cannot make both ends meet. Some of them tell me that every year they have to borrow. I know these men personally. I know that they do not spend one cent needlessly or extravagantly; there is no waste in their households; nothing is spent in liquor, and yet when they come to the end of the year they are obliged to borrow money. These men are the class whom we must 'carefully look after. I do not want to say anything against the high-class people who are paid high salaries, they are paid enough; they look out for themselves. But I think that the Government and the Minister of Finance
should raise the maximum salary in Subdivision B of the Third Class to $1,200 and give an increase of $100 a year without obliging men to go before the Governor in Council to get it, sometimes to see it refused in case it does not suit the deputy head or the chief of the branch to recommend the increase. These men are worth something or they are worth nothing. If they are no good let us drop them from the service right from the start; but those who are good should be well paid.

I think that the Bill to
amend the Civil' Service Act now being considered in committee i-s a fairly generous one. I think that the Minister of Finance is entitled to a great deal of credit for the time and care he has taken with it, especially at this time, when his parliamentary and his national duties must be both numerous and onerous. Speaking for the Civil Service of Ottawa, I think I can say without much exaggeration that it is composed of men and women who are equal to the tasks which they have to perform. They are both energetic and conscientious, and willing to do their duty to the best of their ability. I will admit that there may be cases of inefficiency, but on the whole the Civil Service of Canada, and particularly of Ottawa, is one of which this country has no reason to feel ashamed. I desire to say that what is especially gratifying to me in this Act is the fact that the academic examination prescribed under the Act of 1908 as to qualifying one for promotion from the Third to the Second Division has been done away with, because I always looked upon that examination as a hardship and a cruel measure. I would ask the minister if it would not he possible to repeal in subsection 2 of section 26 the following:-
And who had theretofore passed the qualifying examination.
I think that many men, without passing the qualifying examination, have fitted themselves, by their experience and the acquirement of efficiency in their work, for promotion from the Third to the Second Division. Is it possible to make the statutory increase in the lower grades $100 instead of $50? A man receiving a salary of $600 has to wait eight years before he reaches his maximum. He is, therefore, badly handicapped, especially if the cost of living continues to increase. Is it the intention of the minister to grant the regular statutory increases to men in the service who have gone to the front? I think that when those men come back they should



receive any increases which they would have received had they remained in Canada and performed their duties as civil servants. The least we can do for them is not to let them suffer under any discrimination because they have gone to the front to perform the most patriotic work that a Canadian can be engaged in during this crisjs in our history.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Those who are on service overseas will receive the statutory increases which they would have received had they remained here. In other words, they will find themselves when they return in at least as good a position as they would have occupied had they remained here and got the advance from year to year. As to whether all those in the Third Division could be rendered eligible for promotion upon the certificate of the deputy, I think not; for the reason that it would practically destroy the basis of the present Civil Service Act. The present Act is based on what is known as the merit system; it provides for examination as qualification for promotion from the Third to the Second Division. The amendment provided in section 2 is designed to remove what was clearly an injustice to those who had passed the qualifying examination under the legislation which existed prior to (the fcoming into effect of the Civil Service Act of 1908. But those who were legislated into that division by the Civil Service Act of 1908 or came in since, came in with their eyes open and subject to all the conditions imposed by that Act, among which was the passing of an examination to qualify for entry into the Second Division. I do not believe it would be wise to destroy the basis of the legislation of 1908. If that legislation is unsound, it should be repealed, buit we should not create an anomalous situation by allowing those who passed no examination either before or since the passing of the Act to be eligible for promotion to the Second Division. By this legislation we are giving decided advantages to those at present in the Third Division, and to messengers, sorters and packers. We had it in mind that those receiving less than $1,000 were especially in need of assistance at this time. To those receiving less than $1,000 we are giving a bonus of $100. In addition, the minimum of each of the classes is advanced from $500 to $600, so that a messenger, sorter or packer or a member of the Third Division who is now receiving $500 will be advanced to $600, and will receive, in addition, a

bonus of $100, together with the annual statutory increase of $50. That is to say, a messenger who is receiving $500
5 p,m. will receive for this year $750, an increase of 50 per cent. Moreover, we have provided for an increase in the maximum from $1,200 to $1,300. Those who have reached the former maximum of $1,200 and cannot qualify for promotion to the Second Diyision, can go on to $1,300, whereas under existing legislation they are stopped at $1,200. We think we have met the situation fairly so far as the Third Division is concerned. In order to do this, a very considerable expenditure is involved. When this matter was under consideration the other day the member for St. John asked for a statement as to the cost of the increases authorized by this legislation. I had a statement prepared to meet his request. I find that the total annual increase in expenditure will be, in round figures, $290,000. That is a very substantial annual increase in respect of the Inside Service at Ottawa. It is not too much, but, at the same time, it is substantial. As 1 said the other day, we must bear in mind the public outside and the salaries which they obtain. In the Third Division a number of young women and young men, some of them not specially trained, many of them stenographers, obtain	larger
salaries than are paid outside. I made it my business in connection with this Bill to make inquiries of some of the leading law firms in Toronto as to the salaries paid to stenographers and clerks. I found, of course, considerable difference in the salaries paid, but I am able to say as a result of my inquiry that the salaries paid stenographers in the Civil Service at Ottawa are equal to if not greater than those paid to stenographers in law offices in the city of Toronto, many of whom work much longer hours than those in the Civil Service. While we desire to be fair to the Civil Service, we must at 'the same tjme bear in mind our duty to the general public. I believe that the public are prepared to pay the members of the Civil Service proper salaries, especially those in the lower grades; but I do not believe that they are prepared to pay them larger salaries than are paid to persons possessing similar qualifications who are engaged outside the Civil Service and who work as hard as, if not harder than, those in the Civil Service.

The minister was good enough to lay on the Table the Order in Council to which I have referred relating

to the Civil Service. It is dated May 29, 1917, and is as follows:
