The Committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the Eight Hon. the Prime Minister, advise that all Orders in Council passed since the outbreak of the war relating to Civil Service pay to civil servants who have already enlisted do have no effect and be void in the case of those members of the Civil Service who join the military forces of Canada either by voluntary enlistment or otherwise from and after the date hereof.
Can the minister inform the committee why a discrimination is made against those who voluntarily enlist after May 29?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that the
reason is obvious. Prior to the date in question, the Prime Minister had announced a measure of compulsory military service. It is to be pointed out that the members of the Civil Service who are liable to military service under that measure have had all this time to enlist, and if they have not enlisted, nor offered to enlist, there would seem to be no good ground why they should be paid their full Civil Service pay if that civil pay exceeds their military pay, as distinct from those outside who will be compelled under the Compulsory Service law to serve at the rate of pay provided for in the military forces. I think I can say as to those members of the Service, who are eligible for military service and who offered to enlist prior to the announcement of the Prime Minister, that the Government would be prepared to deal with them by special Orders in Council, so that they might be put in the position of those who actually enlisted before the declaration of the Prime Minister. I think that would he only fair, because I know of some cases in the Civil Service where officials have desired to enlist, but for some ground of public interest, principally because the service they were rendering was of such a character that their services could not well be dispensed with in the public interest, they have been prevented from enlisting. I do not believe there are many of those cases; but I believe there are some, and I know the Government would be prepared to deal with them on the same basis as those who have enlisted and actually gone forward. But as to those who, during all these three years, being eligible for military service, have not come forward and enlisted, it would seem to me to discriminate in their favour as against the outside public if now, being compelled to enlist, they were given the pay which they have as civil servants and which might be fifty per cent in excess
of or twice as great as the pay of those who are not members of the Civil Service and who enlist under the provisions of this measure.

I have noticed in the United States that one of the great objects which those administering the law for selective conscription have in view, is to induce those who are drafted to believe that they are not in any way treated as inferior to those who may volunteer. I think that should be the object of the Government in this country. It ought not to be said to any member of the Civil Service that he is degraded in any way or that, simply because he was taken, if this law passes, under a selective conscription, he occupies an inferior position to that which he would have occupied if he had enlisted voluntarily. If this legislation should pass, the Government should strive in every way to make the young men understand that there is no distinction as between the two classes, and that they are not to be treated as inferior to those who have already gone to the front. But this Order in Council is not limited to those who are taken under selective conscription; it is extended to those who may voluntarily enlist subsequent to the 29th of May. It might well be argued that the intention of the Government was to discourage voluntary enlistment prior to the coming into force of the legislation relating to conscription. What the Government is doing in this regard is on a par with what they did with reference to Col. Blondin and General Lessard. Those gentlemen went down to the province of Quebec-very late, I admit. General Lessard is a man who one would have supposed would have been sent very early into that province; he is the man to whom my hon. friend from Bouville (Mr. Lemieux) two years ago recommended should be employed by the Government to go into the province of Quebec, but quite recently he did go to Quebec with the Postmaster General, and the Postmaster General has stated publicly that voluntary enlistment has succeeded very well, and that if the same methods had been pursued earlier in the war, the young men of Quebec would have rallied en masse to the colours. But instead of waiting for word from General Lessard and Col. Blondin, immediately upon the return of the Prime Minister conscription was announced, and those gentlemen immediately stopped recruiting, because apparently Col. Blondin understood that it was not the desire of the Government that voluntary enlistment should proceed any further*

Whatever may be the fate of the Conscription Bill, the Government should not have 'stopped for one single moment in the direction of voluntary enlistment. Every encouragement should be given to our young men in all the provinces, including the young men in the 'Civil Service, voluntarily to enlist, and there are many people in this country who believe that, if the proper encouragement had been given to all our young men to enlist and proper methods been pursued they would have enlisted in very large numbers, and that possibly compulsory service might not have been necessary at all. I for one am very sorry to see the Government, immediately upon the return of the Prime Minister, bring into force this discriminatory Order in Council under which it is proposed to treat the young men in the Civil Service who may enlist subsequent to the 29th of May in a very much less favourable manner than they have treated those who have enlisted prior to that date. The unfortunate result is that tmen in the Civil Service will be divided into three different classes. We shall have one class of enlisted civil servants who receive both their civil pay and their military pay; we shall have another class who will receive their military pay and the difference between their military and theiT civil pay, and then we shall have a third class wrho will receive only their military pay. Another discriminatory result follows. Those Orders in Council which have been passed previously provide that their positions will be available for the enlisted civil servants when they return from the front. That provision has been,wiped avray by this Order in Council. Throughout the country we find that employers of labour have offered to retain their positions for their young men who enlist; many of the largest business houses and many of the banks have done the 'same thing. They do not discriminate; we find no obstacle in the path of enlistment dating from the announcement of this conscription measure; but today as previously during the years since the war has begun, these employers are prepared to treat their young men in the same generous and liberal manner. But this Government says to the young men in its employ who may offer to enlist after the 29th of May:	You will be treated in a
very much less favourable manner than those who have volunteered before; not only will your pay be reduced, but when you return after you have served your country, possibly maimed and 
wounded, you will find your positions filled by young men who have not volunteered for the front, and you will he obliged to seek occupations amongst strangers. I say that is not fair; it is not wise, it is not in the public interest, it is not giving proper encouragement to the young men of the Civil Service who still continue to volunteer for the defence of the flag.

I concur with the remarks which have been made by my hon. friend from St' John, but I rise more for the purpose of directing the minister's attention to a special case. I regret that the Postmaster General is not in his seat, because he might have been able to give me the information which I sought in yaip when his estimates -were before the House just prior to the adjournment for the Prime Minister's visit to England. The Postmaster General, or in his absence the Minister of Customs, had an item passed by the House creating a new Assistant Deputy Postmaster General. Some years ago, when I was in charge of the department, I appointed a young man who had been secretary to Sir William Mulock. He was one of the best officials that the Post Office Department ever had, but as very often happens with the best men in the Civil Service, he accepted a position outside at a better salary, where the intelligence he displayed in the performance of his duties /was better recognized. Then I appointed in his stead a young man who had been my private secretary. He was then Cpptain Verret, one of the best officers in the Canadian Militia, and a member of the Governor General's Fo'ot Guards. At the opening of hostilities he enlisted with an Ottawa regiment, and immediately went overseas and into the trenches. He has been there since the beginning of the war, has been promoted from captain to major, and only the other day I was proud indeed to read in the papers that he had received from the hand of His Majesty the insignia of the Distinguished Service Order. Major Verret is now at the front and there is nobody here to look after his interest in the department. He was certainly a very good official, highly respected and very popular both in the East and in the West, always accessible, and very genial with all the members of the House of Commons who had occasion to do business with the department. Suddenly, in the third year of the war, after exposing his life on several ocf-casions he is much surprised to learn that another Assistant Deputy Postmaster Gen-

eral has been appointed. I do not say that he has been appointed in Major Verret's stead, but I cannot see why anotner Assistant Deputy Postmaster General should have been appointed during Major Verret's absence. I do not begrudge Mr. Fowler his appointment.' I happen to know him. He is a very good official, although he has not had the long experience of Major Verret. I have told him personally: " I know you are an excellent officer. You are spoken of very highly by the public, but I object to Major Verret being treated in such a highhanded way in his absence, after he has served his King and country on the battlefield for over two years." I have been unable to get an explanation, why another Assistant Deputy Postmaster General was appointed; it may have been that he was needed, and if so, I have no objection to the appointment of Mr. Fowler, none whatever. But what I should like to know is this, and I happen to know that the question is agitating the mind of Major Verret on the battlefield. I dare say that everything possible will be done to promote those men in the Civil Service who return from active service at the front; I think everybody will agree that that is their due. But what I am particularly anxious to know is whether Major Verret, on his return, will be promoted in the department if a vacancy occurs, or will the appointment of another Assistant Deputy Postmaster General have spoilt his chances of promotion? Mr. Fowler is a very able officer, but so is Major Verret, and he has been at the front since the beginning of the war. Should a vacancy occur in his absence, or when he returns, will the Government give him credit for the service he has rendered to the state and promote him? I sincerely regret that the Postmaster General is not in his seat. I did not raise this question when his estimates were before the House just before the two months' adjournment, because I did not want to embarrass the Minister of Customs, who had charge of the Post Office Estimated, but now the Minister of Finance is here, perhaps he will give me the assurance that the absence of Major Verret will not prejudice his chances of promotion should a vacancy occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry I have no information with respect to this matter. I have a rather faint recollection that my hon. friend raised this question some months ago, but as it did not concern my own department, it made no impression upon my mind. I recall, however, that I did make some inquiry about it, rather
casually, and I think I was informed that the appointment my hon. friend refers to was not in the stead of Major Verret. Further than that, I can make no statement, but I would suggest that my hon. friend raise the question where it might more properly be raised-although it was quite proper for him to raise it now-namely, when the Estimates of the Postmaster General are again under consideration.

May we expect the Postmaster General to return to the House? There is a rumour that he is coming back, but has not yet taken his seat because he is occupied elsewhere. If the hon. Minister of Finance can give me assurance on this-point, I will be content.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Postmaster General is on military duty, but when his Estimates are under consideration, either he or an acting minister will be present. The [DOT] hon. gentleman can Taise his question then.

In answer to my remarks in favour of an increase of pay to those in the Third Division, the hon. Minister of Finance stated that there were a great many stenographers in that class who are paid more highly than similar workers are paid in commercial offices. Would it not be possible to make provision in the Bill for a special scale for the stenographers? I understand that the work of the stenographers is not so hard as the clerical work generally, and it is a kind of work that is done usually by girls who have no one to look after but themselves, and who consequently do not need as large salaries as the heads of families do. If the only objection is that which the minister has stated, I think a special class should be made for the stenographers, and they should be removed from the third class entirely.
Bill reported.

On motion of Sir Thomas White the House resumed in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
Arts and Agriculture-Towards the encouragement of cold storage warehouses for the better preservation and handling of perishable food products, $50,000.

['All right.
Progress reported.

On motion of Hon. Mr. Burrell the House adjourned at 11.05 p.m.
Wednesday, June 13, 1917.']

There is a good deal of discussion nowadays about the cold storage houses. It is alleged that they buy up food products and carry them unnecessarily, thereby unduly increasing prices. There

was a time a few years ago when, I think, it was absolutely necessary for the Government to encourage the system of cold storage, but now it' has become a large business. To what class of cold storage concerns does this vote go?

This item was
held over at the instance, I think, of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) after we had quite a discussion on the whole cold storage question, and pending information as to the point the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) had reached in the inquiry which he is now carrying on. I took tire matter up with the Minister pf Labour and learned that he had collected most of the information and expects soon to be able to lay a full report on the Table. In view of the fact that until that report is laid on the Table, the Department of Agriculture will make no new regulations, on the subject, I thought probably there would be no objection on the part of my hon. friend to the passing of this item. I cannot do any more in the matter. In answer to my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) I may say that subsidies will be given as hitherto. Only pne subsidy will be given in a district, and on certain condition. The plans and specifications must be accepted by the department; ample space must be afforded for public cold storage; and the rates must be under control of the department. On these conditions thirty per cent pf the cost of construction is given in payrpents spread over five years. We have not been giving many subsidies and have rather intended not to give more during the war. Besides, as a matter of fact, the country has been pretty well covered and the accommodation of the public in regard to cpld storage provided for. Formerly this vote was $200,000, and now it is down to $50,000.

I suppose the minister
takes care not to encourage the establishment of cold storage houses where they are not needed for the public?
Yes. And besides we dp not give the subsidy to any body without assurance that ample room for public cold storage will be provided.

That is, space where the public can store goods on paying certain rates? Spmebody suggested the other night that the charge for cold storage was very high. I think it was said that eggs were charged for at the rate of 12 cents a dozen. Did the minister look into that? I thought

the statement absurd but I did not have the knowledge to refute it.

I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend the exact figure but it cannot be that. It may vary a little in different localities. As a matter of fact, our officers look over these rates very carefully and if there is the slightest complaint on the part of the public, or if the rate charged seems to be exorbitant, we have the power to reduce the rate, and we have exercised it. I think you will find that the rates are those generally accepted by the trade.
You would not have the power of reducing the rate charged by a private cold storage? ,

If it is a cold storage to which we give a subsidy.
Mr. MeMILLAN: Is it the intention of the Government to have the duty removed from oleomargarine coming into Canada?

It is not a question of duty, but there is a provision on the statute book prohibiting the manufacture or importation of oleomargarine. The Government has had this question under consideration, we have had a very voluminous correspondence but I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend any satisfaction.
The statement has been published that this question is such a controversial one that the Government intend to submit it to the judgment of the House. May I ask the minister if that is the intention?

Quite naturally, anything that is brought up in the way of legislation is submitted to the judgment of the House. This subject like a great many others, would probably be elucidated by being aired. There has not been, as far as my knowledge goes, anything like a controversial discussion about the matter recently. There was during the winter. I could not give my hon. friend any satisfaction as to what the Government may or may not do.
Mr. MeMILLAN: I think this is a question that requires serious consideration at this time.because we know that people in towns and cities are in a very serious condition. Labouring men and poor people are finding it very difficult to get along because of the high cost of living. I live in a dairy country and ninety per cent of the people I represent are farmers who depend upon dairying entirely. I would have been quite prepared to have supported any measure

brought down by this Government to allow the importation of oleomargarine during the continuance of the war that poor people might at least have oleomargarine to put upon their bread instead of being obliged to eat it dry. But the price which has been fixed for cheese in this country has been disappointing to myself and.to most of the farmers. If the Government had arranged to have a larger price fixed for cheese, say about 25 cents, we could have afforded to have advocated the admission of oleomargarine for the benefit of the labouring people and anybody else who chose to eat it. But I believe it would not be fair on account of the low price of 21f cents fixed for cheese to be sold to the British Commission. That price only means between 19 and 20 cents a pound to the farmers. In considering the price of farm products we must take into account the high cost of everything that the farmer is obliged to use. A self-binder that he used to buy for $130 now costs $165, and many other articles, including cream separators, wagons, and implements generally, have gone up from 10 to 25 per cent, -as well as the feed that he has to bhy for his cattle. Last year our cheese averaged 19 cents a pound, and it will be about the same this year. On account of the high cost of everything that the farmer has to- buy I think the Government should -have arranged a higher price -for his cheese. He should get three or four cents a pound more for it. If the Government had secured such a price we could have -allowed the poor people in the towns and cities to have used oleomargarine.

I have had some more resolutions from a number of dairymen's associations in Southwestern Ontario in reference to the inspection of -cheese -at Montreal. They want inspectors appointed for the district west of Toronto, which is a very laTge and important cheese-making district. I do- not want to weary the .minister with something that he cannot control, but I, think that he -might possibly have some control over this question and arrange this matter satisfactorily to the dairymen of southwestern Ontario. I understood from the' -buyer that they were paying more -for cheese on the other side than they are on this 6dde. He was buying in Illinois and Wisconsin and he told me he was paying more to the cheese factory there than he- was paying on this side.
For export?
Yes, because he talked to me about being able to get vessels in New York when he could not get them in Montreal.

I have already directed the attention of the commission to unis subject which my hon. friend has brought before me. I have had one or two letters along the same line. Obviously, although my hon. friend may be pretty nearly right in saying that I -could bring this to the attention of the commission, it is not desirable for me to be butting in in the way of trying to control their operations. I am very glad to bring anything of this kind to the attention of the commission, and I am quite positive that they will do their best to solve -all these questions in such a manner as to eliminate all possible friction that can be eliminated. I would like to say to my hon. friend from Glengarry (Mr. McMillan) that if he could know all that is taking place, which he cannot, because necessarily there are confidential communications to a certain extent between the British authorities and myself, I am sure that he would agree that everything possible, in so far as this Government is concerned, has been done in this cheese business to try and get the fullest attention paid to the interests of the producers of this country. But, it is not a question of what we have done. We could not say to the British authorities: You must pay so-and-so for the cheese you get in this country. All we could say to them was that we wanted them to give the fullest consideration to those points which my hon. friend has raised. One contention of the hon. gentleman I quite admit, namely, that the cost of production to the farmers has gone up, and that conditions are not what they were. We have pointed out in the strongest way to the British authorities that if they are desirous of securing the export of the surplus cheese in Canada for the use of the army and the population of Great Britain, it is necessary for them to remember that they must give such a price as would induce the people to manufacture cheese and not turn the raw material in ' other directions. We pressed that on them strongly and persistently. With regard to the other point that the hon. gentleman raises, this also was remembered, and I think it is most desirable that a state of things should not exist-I do not think i-t will exist-under which the American exporter will be able to pay a larger price for cheese than they are paying in Canada and

export at a larger figure to the Old Country than the figure at which they are buying through the commission. I have already brought that point to the attention of the British Commission, and I shall be very glad to emphasize it further.	.
My information is not gossip, you know; it is absolutely direct.

No. Of course, my hon. friend knows that the local conditions will always vary. It does not follow that because local prices in the United States may be. higher than here, the export prices are higher. The export price usually has been the same, because the cheese from the United States has formed only one per cent of the exportable cheese of this continent. It is a bagatelle -compared with our own cheese. The price of our cheese has been the ruling factor in the export trade, and I think it will be in this case also. I know that the shipping question has been -a very difficult and acute one. I understand from the British authorities that they have not been making any discrimination. It is quite possible that now and then when a boat sailing from New York missed a load of munitions, or something of that kind, they filled up with Cheese, but I do not believe they make a practice of taking cheese from American ports and not from Canadian ports. We have taken every conceivable step to get the fullest justice done to the producers of this country, while at the same time giving the British -authorities all the cheese we could.
Does my hon. friend expect that the price fixed by the British Board of Trade will remain the same throughout the season, 2I| cents f.o.b., Montreal?

It is not a matter over which I have any control or in reference to which I could make any positive statement. I -can only say that I understand the British Commission had instructions to buy for a fortnight, -but apparently the price was left open. I earnestly appealed to them to fix a price as -high as possible, and it would be very desirable not to lower that price. If the conditions w-arrant it, as they may later on towards the fall, the price might be increased, but, so far as we are concerned, we will do all we can to see that the price is not lowered.

My understanding is that no cheese manufacturers in thi-s country are compelled to. sell their cheese through this channel.
[Mr. Burrell 1
Who else would they sell it to?
I do not see why a cheese dealer should go to the United States and pay a higher price for cheese there and ship via New York if he could buy in this country at a greater advantage to himself.
They could not bring it in here.

They could ship Canadian cheese through New York just as easily as they could American. So I think the instances which the hon. -member for North Oxford gives have been special and exceptional cases. I think it would be well for our cheese manufacturers to fully appreciate the difficulties of the situation and not pay too much attention to a campaign which seems to be put up in Ontario to discourage farmers and get them dissatisfied with what has been done by 'the British Government . through its commission. They are being told that they will have to wait a long time for their pay. As I understand, there will be no great delay, the cheese will be paid for on presentation of warehouse receipts. They are told that hooping with steel hoops will cost much more. I understand that will be paid for by the commission, and not taken out of the producers. In fact, it is simply transferring the British market from the Old Country to Montreal, and the producers of cheese in this country will be delivering their cheese to the British Government at Montreal instead of to the dealers in England and Scotland. I am sure that the farmers and dairymen will be very well satisfied with the regulations when they understand them. As to the price, prices are never high enough for some people, and it is a question whether 21| cents is high enough; but so far as the regulations are concerned, I do not think there is any reason why the farmers and producers should feel dissatisfied.

The friend of whom I
spoke is a -cheese buyer not only in Canada but in the United States. He has a firm in the United -States as well as in Canada, and is a very large buyer. He knows exactly what he can do without my hon. friend (Mr. Steel-e) telling him anything. He has been in the -business a number of years, and is just as anxious to'pay a price to the Canadian as to the American cheese makers. As a matter of fact, for some reason., he could pay a higher price. to the American than to the Canadian producer,

and he could get space for all the cheese he wanted to ship through New York and could not possibly get any space from Canada at that time, and that was only a week ago last Monday night. My friend absolutely knows his business, there is no possible question about that. There is no discussion up with us as to delay in getting paid for cheese. There is a little longer delay because it has to be delivered at Montreal whereas the ordinary cheese buyer on our markets pays for the cheese the day it is delivered, inspects it at the factory and pays for it when it is delivered. It is quite possible that the minister can secure some arrangement under which the cheese will be inspected in the West. If that is done, from what I have heard, it will do away largely with any complaint with reference to the British Government taking over this cheese. As to the price, I have not the slightest hesitation in thinking that if they dq not get the cheese at the price they will pay more for it. They will pay the price to get it, that stands .to common sense. However, 21J cents, or 19 cents to the factory, is a pretty fair price at this time of the year. It is more than the price at this time last year. Therefore, I do not think the producers are suffering in that way. If the farmers will not send the milk to the cheese factories, then the British Commission will have to pay a price that will induce them to send it to the cheese factories, that is all there is to that.

Have any definite arrangements been made by this Government with the Imperial Government and the Government of the United States with reference to the proportion of the aid which Canada is expected to give to Great Britain and the Allies in connection with food supplies of various kinds? In the Imperial House of Commons statements have been made by under-secretaries in answer to questions as to the reliance of Great Britain and the Allies on the 'continent of North America for food supplies, and I understand that some arrangements have been arrived at by the United States as regards quantities and other details. Has anything been done by the Canadian Government, and if so, along what lines.

I do not think there have been any special arrangements. The matter has been discussed from time to time. I do not think anything clear-cut has yet been evolved .in the United States, because the Government are waiting for powers to deal with these matters. They are asking for rather, strong powers and making their general arrangements, and when they secure those powers, it is anticipated that, as far as feasible, we shall work in co-operation with them. I do not think that I can say anything more definite than that at the present time.

I am rather in the dark as to matters that may impinge upon the realm of diplomacy, but the necessity of furnishing to Great Britain and the Allies supplies, not merely of wheat and flour, but of other kinds of food, is apparent. From time to time, some of the home authorities have' declared that the assurance of food supplies is essential above everything else. The statement has been made in the Imperial House of Commons as to understandings having been arrived at with the executive of the United States, and that executive have submitted to Congress a Bill asking for certain definite powers in reference to it, no doubt on the basis of some general understanding. Has the Canadian Government arrived at any such understanding?

Except in a general way; there is nothing that 1 would be able to tell my hon. friend of a definite character at the present time.

Some months ago I
called to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is always kind and genial, a project of reciprocal exhibitions between France and Canada. About two years ago, the French Government sent to America a commission composed of business men and some members of the House of Representatives. That commission wa3 headed by Mr. D'Amours, deputy of the Department of Landes, France. Mr. D'Amours, I believe, was the vice-president of the commission on trade in the French Parliament. That commission visited all the business centres in the United States and then came to Canada. I was present in Montreal at various gatherings which were convened * for the purpose of explaining the object of that commission. The French Government had in view the development of better trade relations between the outside world and France. As the president of the commission, Mr. D'Amours, truly said: We do not wish to be surprised by peace as we have been surprised by war. He published broadcast in the United States and in Canada what statistics he had in his possession as to the trade of France previous to the war with Germany, which trade could be transferred to America, and notably to Canada. He gave a list of different articles which could be bought in Canada as cheaply as in Germany. Let me give one instance. He stated, much to the surprise of the merchants, manufacturers and business men who were present, that all of the asbestos bought by the French manufacturers or by the French Government-and it represents a very large quantity-had been imported from Germany, while Germany imported nearly all the asbestos from Canada. He said: "Our commission merchants were in Berlin 'whilst they should have been in Canada." After the visit of the commission, a delegation of business men was invited to visit France and to tour the principal industrial centres. That delegation was composed of the members of the Boards of Trade of Montreal, Quebec, and Toronto. The president of the delegation, was, 1 think, Mr. Woods, president of the Toronto Board of Trade. That delegation went into all parts of France. Senator Beaubien, who has taken a very lively interest,in this matter, accompanied the delegation at his own expense, and on his return he published a very exhaustive report of what the delegation had seen on the other side. The correspondence is in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and it is made clear that we can very

.materially increase our trade with France. What struck me in discussing this item of exhibitions is this:
Senator Beaubien and Mr. Woods were approached while they were in France by officials of the French Government and by representatives of the boards of trade of the larger cities, such as Lyon, Bordeaux, Havre, Rouen, and 'Marseilles, and a plan was evolved for a train exhibition of the products of both countries. If the Canadian Government could arrange with our traders and manufacturers for an exhibition of our staple products and samples of our industrial work the French Government agreed to equip a train to display the goods, running, let us say, between Havre and Marseilles, and to pay all the expenses. Trains of this sort have been formerly used in Ca/nada, giving our people an opportunity to become acquainted with the natural and industrial products of the country. The French Government, on the other hand, agreed that if the Canadian Government would equip a similar train to run through our provinces from ocean to ocean, they would arrange with their manufacturers- for a similar display of French products and manufactured goods. It was hoped that by this plan the trade of both countries would be fostered and greatly encouraged. I do not know whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce has consulted with the Minister of Agriculture about this matter, or whether he has come to any decision, but in view of the conditions that will arise in the post-bellum days I think it would be in the interest of both countries if this excellent idea were carried out. We have at the present time a very important and very large trade with France, and there is no reason why it should not be developed and maintained, especially in view of the revelations that were made by the French Commission when they visited this country, and which showed such glaringly foolish transactions as the purchase of asbestos in Berlin by French consumers when it could have 'been easily procured in Canada, which produces such large quantities.
The minister has been successful in the last two exhibitions in which Canada participated, and I think if he would give some thought to this project of the French Government and of the French Chambers of Commerce he would render a great service to the business men of this country. It may be that when the Estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce are up I shall enlarge upon this subject, because I have copies of some very interesting and
illuminating correspondence between business men in France and Senator Beaubien and Mr. Woods. Our duty at the present moment is certainly to do as much as we can to win the war, but we must not lose sight of what is to happen after the war, and one of the chief duties of the Government, it seems to me, is to prepare to capture trade during the period immediately following the war. We will need wider markets, and what better foreign market is there than that of France? I think if an exhibition train of this sort could be equipped and put into commission it would render a very great service to the business men of this country.

I have a very fair recollection of what transpired in the negotiations to which my hon. friend has alluded, in which, though my department was not directly concerned I took a very sympathetic interest. I cannot say just how far the negotiations went or whether the matter was definitely dropped or not. I know, however, that it was taken up in some detail, and that some of the circumstances are as my hon. friend has described. The matter was discussed at some length, I believe, by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, because it would naturally be done largely under their auspices, or at all events the merchandise would be collected for the train by their machinery, and that would involve a great deal of preparation. I stated that if the project came to any definite conclusion my department should be glad to help in any way in connection with our own exhibition work, although it was entirely out of our line to deal with a train of this sort. I rather think the project was dropped, whether by mutual agreement or not I do not know, on account of the terrific pressure of the war, which made it inadvisable to go on with the scheme. That is my understanding, but no doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be able to give my hon. friend a fuller explanation.

Therefore onl-y one French-Canadian of nineteen employees-, while the French element in -the Dominion, according to the census of 1911, aggregates, I think, 28 or 30 per cent of the whole population; the proportion would likely -be greater to-day. It does occur to ime that the French-Can-adians should be represented in the Department of Agriculture in proportion to their number. Since conditions have not improved, I deem it my duty to -draw the attention of the minister to that matter, as I have done in this House for some years; miy object in discussing the matter publicly to-night is to bring it to the notice of the minister, that he may take the first opportunity of remedying -that grievance and granting ns the fair treatment to which we are entitled and which would work to the benefit of agriculture. I think I have said enough to convince the minister that for all those reasons we

are entitled to fair treatment and, if (he has not caught my meaning, I am quite willing to repeat (briefly in .English what I have just said in French.

Had my hon. friend (Mr. Boulay), who speaks English very well, addressed the committee in that language, he would have made himself more intel-ligble to me, and I should have been able to follow him with greater clearness, because I am not, I regret to- say, so well acquainted with the French language as I might be. Dr. Mou-tizambert, for instance, would be able to follow my hon. friend no matter how long lie might speak French, and he would be able to. reply to him with absolute, clearness in that language. Mr. Doherty, Mr. Grisdale, Mr. Lynch, Mr. Charlan, also, are very familiar with the French language. In fact, Dr. Grisdale, who occupies the very important position of Director of Experimental Farms-I understood my hon. friend to say that agriculture was not receiving the attention it should receive from the Federal Government, in that officers who do not understand French are sent out to address the public-could go before an audience of French-Oanadians and address them in their own language with absolute facility. So, I cannot altogether plead guilty to the hon. gentleman's accusation. Perhaps he had better tackle some bther minister.
But we do not see those who talk French.

That may be because
they are there when the hon. gentleman is not at home, but officers who speak French visit Iris section of the country with fair frequency. It is true that we have not so many technical officers in t'he service as we should like to have who understand French thoroughly; but I would point out that in this country the most highly- trained agricultural students, are, unfortunately, not graduated from the colleges m which French is the language.
This Government has probably done more to strengthen the agricultural colleges of Quebec than all preceding Governments. The hon. gentleman may or may not know that for the last four years, under the Agricultural Instruction Act, we have given
$20,000 to Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, and also to Oka College, for the express purpose of strengthening the staffs and equipment of those French Canadian colleges, in agriculture, in order' that they may turn out more highly equipped students, whom we would gladly employ. But I am bound to say, and without prejudice in the matter, that no one who knows thoroughly the science and practice of agriculture would say that either of the institutions I have mentioned could turn out half as many practically trained students in agriculture as an institution like the college at Guelph. In our wqrk we must have men who not only have a practical knowledge of agriculture, but who also understand the scientific basis of their calling; and for this class of men we have to look almost entirely to such institutions, and largely to the institution at' Guelph. With the work we have been doing for the last four years we hope in future to have a larger choice of men. We hope to continue that work for some years to come, if we stay in power; and even if, to the misfortune of the country, we do not stay in power, the 'succeeding Government, whatever it may be, I am sure, will not upset the work done under the authority of the Agricultural Instruction Act.
That work will still go on. When that work comes to fruition and when these educational institutions are sufficiently strengthened that they will turn out a large number of young men -who will not only understand the French and English languages but who will be thoroughly equipped in scientific agriculture, if I am in charge of this depaitment, I will be only too glad to secure the services of such men. But, in the meantime, I must frankly say I have great difficulty in getting hold of men who thoroughly understand both the French and English language. I do not know that this has any special reference to the item under discussion which is our exhibition work. In connectiorf with this work, I might say that we have not very much of a staff but we have no less than three men who are on the permanent staff who are French-Canadians and who also have a thorough acquaintance with the English language. As to the work of the commish sioner, I confess Col. Hutcheson does not understand French, or to a very slight extent, but, although I did not appoint him, and although he was appointed by the late Government, I am bound to say that if you were to search from one end of Canada to the other, I do not think you could conceivably find a man who could take Mr. COMMONS
Hutcheson's place in connection with exhibition work. He has been in the service for sixteen or seventeen years. Not only by his marvellous natural capacity for exhibition work, but also by his long experience in international exhibitions, he has achieved an almost unrivalled supremacy in connection with big international exhibitions. Hutcheson as commissioner, I think he would have been more than satisfied that it would be almost impossible to get any man in this country who would be equally capable in that class of work. I understand that new regulations have been promulgated by the department presided over by the hon. the Minister of Agriculture, and from information I have received, it would appear that these rules will entirely disrupt a lifelong practice in regard to the manufacture, boxing and curing of cheese in Western Ontario, and I believe also in Eastern Ontario. In the county that I have the honour to represent we have a very large number of cheese factories. In one township of that county alone there are nine factories within the confines of the township and four on the border or, in other words, Elma, a township of 67,000 acres, contains within it nine factories, with four on the border, serving the patrons of these 67,000 acres, or a factory to every 5,000 acres, which is probably one of the most densely covered cheese manufacturing districts in the country. We have practically

This practice is followed by the stock merchants of the country, as well as by the abattoir	companies.	A	statement I	have here shows	that thenumber	of hogs	purchased	and	soldin Canada for the year ending March 31,	1916, was 2,363,693, which at theaverage	price of	hogs for	the	year,

One-half of one per cent .on the value of the hogs purchased in that year would amount to $290,000. This is the amount collected by the abbatoirs. So there was a clear gain to these different concerns of over $125,000. This amount the abattoirs and commission purchasing houses have extracted from the pockets of the farmers. Feeling that the department is anxious to have this matter rectified, I would suggest to the minister that it would be only fair to take
it up with these different concerns. If they are going to continue to Tob the public as in the past, it might he advisable for the department to take over the hogs that are condemned at a price and compel the abattoirs to cease altogether this unfair charge.
I should he glad if the minister would give this his most serious attention and, if possible, find some means to stop the unfair practice that is going on.	.

This matter has come to our attention .once or twice before, but I shall he glad to take it up again. It is easy for these concerns, of course, to make up the statement in the form my hon. friend has mentioned, hut it has a misleading effect so far as the owner of the hogs is concerned, because it leads him to think that they are transferring to him a charge that they have to pay to us. Would it he possible, if
they continue making this charge against the producer, to provide for it in some way in these Estimates? It seems most unjust that the abbatoirs should reap a harvest in this unfair manner. Was there much animal
disease in the country last year-much cholera among hogs or glanders among horses? Or what were the principal troubles?	>

The situation as to the disease among our herds is very much better than it has ever been before in the history of the country. In glanders, whereas in 1913-14 the sum of $34,000 was paid for compensation for animals slaughtered, this has gradually worked down until last year we paid only $20,709. Hog cholera, which four years ago cost us $61,000, and the following year $190,000, we have cut down to the lowest point in the country's experience

-$27,000, involving the destruction of 4,400 animals. Dourine, with 'which we had great trouble in the West-hon. members from Alberta will know about it-cost us at one time $48,000, later $32,000; and now it is down to only $3,900 for the killing of 32 animals. This means that the disease is practically under control. Altogether, so far as all these scheduled diseases go, the country never was in a better condition than at present.

I congratulate the minister and his department on that happy condition. I understood-I do not now recall the source of my information-that the minister had circularized the country to the effect that he was paying some compensation for the slaughter of cattle affected with tuberculosis.

Two or three years ago we took up the question of bovine tuberculosis, in the hope of reducing it, if not eradicating it completely. It is" a very, difficult subject, as the hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt) knows. We passed Regulations by which we could take up with any of the municipalities, which number over 5,000, the question of trying to eliminate tuberculosis in the herds that supply the dairies of the cities. We took it up in this way, "because we' thought the first step to be taken should be to protect the people in the cities who- especially the children-are rather helpless in regard to contaminated and infected milk. But the only city that went into this work thoroughly was the city of Saskatoon. The authorities of that city took .advantage of our regulations. These regulations provide . that the city must have a sanitary inspector of the dairies, to compel conformity with the conditions we have laid down as to the space to be allowed for each animal, the light, ventilation, and so on. Then we would, from time to time, subject the cattle to the tuberculin test and destroy reactors or separate them, giving their owners certain compensation. The difficulty was that the compensation was not quite enough. We found that it would be more helpful towards the desired end if we increased the amount of compensation so that men owning infected cattle would not be so much afraid to come in and take advantage of our inspection. Also, we made provision in reference to the herds that were not entirely free from tuberculosis, .that the milk might be sold so long as it vras pasteurized, as pasteurizing eliminates the possibility of transmittiing the tuberculosis from the

bovine to the human form. Under these regulations, passed a couple of months ago, we expected to have a number of municipalities take up the work in conjunction with the department and regulate the business as in Saskatoon, where they have brought the whole thing down to less than two per cent.
What amount is allowed for each animal now?
We allow $40. Before that- we allowed one-third of the maximum valuation, which is $60. Afterwards we raised it to two-thirds, and, as the owner has the salvage, he .may realize the full amount.

It is unfortunate in the
interest of the public health that municipalities did not more generally avail themselves of the assistance which the Government afforded towards eradicating tuberculosis among the herds in their several districts. What method has been adopted of .acquainting the municipalities which are eligible for assistance under this Act of the changed conditions? I think it has been evident in the past that while the Government has attempted to lend assistance, that assistance has not been attractive enough to encourage the municipalities to take any interest in it, largely by reason of the inadequate compensation. The conditions having been Changed during the past month or two, I would think it very important, if the municipalities are to- avail themselves of the assistance offered by the Government, that they should be properly acquainted with the conditions.
Not only were the regulations published in the Gazette, but we also circularized the medical health officers of all the municipalities.
In addition to the municipalities, do the department take it up with individual farmers? Will they pay compensation to an individual farmer if he takes that means of ridding his herd of tuberculosis?

That is a very big undertaking to start at the present time. The best we can do .at the present time is to deal with the municipalities. If we started with individuals it would become a tremendous task. That would be the most practical step in the education looking to the eradication of bovine tuberculosis in Canada, but no country in the world has adopted it. If we were to make it com-

pulsory for the province of Ontario, alone we would get into enormous difficulties.

My suggestion was not
that you should make it compulsory, but suppose you let is he known to individual farmers that you would pay an indemnity of, say, $40 for each animal slaughtered, the farmer would report oases themselves. I understand that the department still supplies tuberculin to individual farmers who send for it?
Yes.

In that case the farmer
might take it up himself if he knew he would be compensated for the cattle he would have to slaughter. I do not mean that the department should use compulsion. But, as you know, a great many cattle that are .affected with tuberculosis are sold for what are called eanners and cutters. I do not know that that is a very nice thing to make bully beef out of, but still there are a great, many cattle of that class picked up by drovers and sold to the canning factory.

Of course, the tuberculous cattle that my hon. friend is referring to would be condemned in the abattoir although they, would not be if they were sold to the ordinary butcher. The provinces and municipalities cannot disassociate themselves from responsibility in this matter because they have power, with ourselves to deal with the question locally. We supply tuberculin to test animals to any farmer who wants to find out if he has tuberculous cattle. It is quite true that we have not paid compensation for the reason that if we started that we do not knew where it would end. In British Columbia the Provincial Government took it up as a domestic question and they passed an Act providing for the inspection, slaughter and compensation of animals. It is open to any province, or any district, to do it, but it would be a task of tremendous magnitude to go as far as iny hon. [DOT]friend suggests. We have already taken one step forward and I do not say that we will not take another.
There must be some way of getting around the inspection. My hon. friend says that cattle affected with tuberculosis would be condemned at the abattoir?
Yes.
As a matter of fact, the cattle are shipped to the abattoir.
They are condemned.
The drover is like the rest of us; he would not continue to buy cattle liable to be condemned, and which would entail loss. The drovers do buy such cattle and they ship them to the abattoir.
The percentage of cattle condemned is of course not so large as the case of hogs.
Only the parts affected are condemned?
Yes.
Part of the beast might pass inspection and the part that is affected would be condemned?
Yes.

Has the serum treatment been used by the officers of the department as a preventitive against hog cholera, if so, has it proved satisfactory, and can the minister give the committee an idea of how many hogs ha-ve been treated during the past year and what saving was made?

It has'been very satisfactory. The saving to the department would probably be about $35,000 last year as a result of applying the serum treatment to contact hogs. In a district in which hog cholera has broken out we condemn those affected with the disease, treat the contacts and if necessary they are slaughtered on the premises.
Have steps been taken to prevent the feeding of garbage to hogs unless the garbage has been treated?

Yes, I would say to my hon. friend that in the last two years the majority of the outbreaks of hog. cholera have been directly traceable to the feeding of uncooked garbage. In the United States, where they inoculate altogether and do not slaughter as we do, it has been found that a hog may be immune and yet he may be absolutely a carrier of disease. If uncooked garbage containing the germs of the disease are fed to hogs it will transmit hog cholera and in the majority of cases we have found it directly traceable to the feeding of uncooked garbage. Last year we framed regulations providing that no man should feed uncooked garbage, or if he did, he would run the risk of having no compensation at all. That has had its effect. We have gone a little further and now we have instituted a system of licenses so that no man can feed, any garbage of this kind unless he is licensed and the officers of the department

I would suggest to the Minister that he take steps to give wider distribution to the publications of his department, particularly those showing the results of successful experiments and . of good business practice, in regard to stock raising, and other branches of farming.

The Publications Branch as it stands at present is a connecting link between the Department of Agriculture and the public. By its operations the agricultural community and all interested are provided with the annual and other reports of the several branches, as well as with the pamphlet booklets, circulars, leaflets, and similar publications issued under the auspices of the department. During the past few years, the system of distribution has been improved and the volume of circulation much increased. A little time ago each branch of the Agricultural Department issued its own publications and

paid for them-ran its own show, as it were. These have all been consolidated now under a speciai branch, the Publications Branch. Until the present system was organized in 1912 each branch distributed its -own publications. The lists were small and much of the addressing was done by hand. These lists, involving French and division lists numbering twenty-seven, included about 150,000 English and French names. The lists have been since that consolidated, reclassified and developed until upwards of 306,000 people are receiving our bulletins, and are directly reached by the information afforded by investigation, research and study at the experimental farms and the livestock, dairy and other branches. For the development of the live stock industry, $700,000.
What steps .is the minister taking towards the development of the live stock industry?

Development is taking place along a great many lines. For instance, two years ago we inaugurated a plan of giving assistance to fairs. The live stock interests were exceedingly anxious that the Government should supply a large-amount of money for the establishment of a large central live stock show, a'long the lines of that held from time to time in Chicago. They came 'to us with a proposal that would involve an expenditure of $250,000 or more. We looked into the matter carefully, and I told the various delegations that before we would undertake to do anything it would be neces-
10 p.m. sary that the live stock interests *throughout the country should be harmonized. That is, they should agree upon a method and upon a place where the proposed fair should be held. The further they went the more difficult it became to reconcile the different interests concerned. Having regard to our geographical conditions, naturally it was difficult for them to agree upon a central place for the holding of the exhibition. Finally it seemed that the whole project would break down, and as we were convinced that it was desirable to assist the development of the live stock industry, we laid down a plan under whieh any exhibition that had given a prize list of $5,000 for the utility classes of live stock in a previous year should get a grant of $2,500 to assist that feature of the fair. We agreed to give half the amount of their przie list in the previous year, limiting the amount to $5,000. Speaking off-hand, about twenty or thirty fairs throughout the country took advantage of th^s provision, which has been operating during the last three years, and still ' continues. Owing to the war conditions, and, in some cases, to the buildings being taken up by the military authorities, some of the fairs have found it difficult to continue their work. We are trying, however, to encourage it; we do not think that it should be dropped. This year we are reducing the amount which must have been given in prizes on a previous year, with a view to giving more assistance to the winter and spring shows, which are confined to the exhibition of the utility classes of livestock. Probably we shall reduce the amount to $2,500, so that any livestock fair, which, in a previous year, gave prizes amounting

to $2,500 will receive another $2,500 to assist that feature of their show. This applies to those shows which have no other attraction than that of livestock, and which do not strongly attract those members of the public who are not interested in livestock.

It is rumoured that the department sometimes sends stock to various localities to encourage the breeding of better animals, and that sometimes this stock is not used for breeding purposes. I heard the other day 'about somebody Who was ploughing with a bull that my hon. friend sent out. Has the minister ever heard of anything of that kind being done? Is there much buying of sires for localities and giving them to those localities dree?

Without dealing with this special case mentioned by my hon. friend of a bull ploughing-although that is very good work in these .days-we did establish about three or four years ago-and it was work in which Mr. John Bright was very much interested-the practice, for improving the herds of Canada, of the department purchasing pure bred sires, and then when associations were formed to undertake the maintenance and care of the animals, we would lend them to them under certain regulations which were promulgated by the department and assented to by the associations. Under that policy which has been under way for about three years-this is the fourth year-we have distributed throughout Canada more than 3,000 animals, that is, bulls, stallions, rams and boars. There were about 1,200 bulls altogether. A great number of these have gone to outlying points of the community or to backward portions of the various provinces where the herds have been of a very poor class, where inbreeding has been practised, where scrub bulls have been running around at large and all that sort .of thing, so that the livestock industry of those particular sections, instead of being built up on sound, progressive lines, has been the reverse. If I had time, I do not think I would have difficulty in showing that this work* has been immensely appreciated throughout the country,' and that it has done an immense amount of good. The hon. member can quite understand that, in the distribution throughout all parts of the country of 3,000 animals, during a period of three or four years, in certain parts of the country where the people are not intelligent there is some difficulty in having the regulations lived up to. It is true that

in the province of Quebec, to which the hon. member probably, alludes, in the case of one or two associations we did have a little trouble where the people were particularly ignorant and did not appear to understand the regulations. Is it the policy of the department to pay the same contribution towards racing or trotting stock as for general purpose horses?

We make no distinction between breeds. There was a suggestion at one time that we should contribute more for' thoroughbreds with the idea of encouraging the raising of remounts, but we have got it down now to a basis of 40 per cent for all breeds, and it remains for the associations to specify the particular breed they want.
If an association in an outlying district wants a thoroughbred sire, have they to send for it or is the horse shipped to them?

I do not want my hon. friend to confuse the two things. In the first place we are ourselves buying and distributing pure bred stallions, and associations are formed to maintain and take care of them. But this is another form of

assistance, by which people who form clubs can get any individual animal they desire, we assisting by paying 40 per cent of the service fee.

I do not wish to discourage the minister in his efforts to improve the live stock of this country, but there have been brought to my attention certain conditions bearing on the one principle of assistance that he mentioned which I think it is only right I should bring before the minister. When the Government undertakes to supply thoroughbred sires, either cattle or horses, they to a large extent debar local enterprise. It may be said that it is not a matter of concern to the Government whether local enterprise is encouraged or discouraged, but when the Government undertakes to meet the needs of the country in this way, it is absolutely necessary that the stock so furnished should be of a satisfactory character. It is not a benefit to the country for the Government to provide sires of anything but the highest class. By providing sires that are not of a high quality, they at one and the same time deter home enterprise and fail to build up the stock of the country in the way that is desired. I am sorry to say that my information is that in too many cases sires of inferior breed, both cattle and horses, have been sent into different parts of the West. 'I do not wish to make an allegation, but I think it is only right that I should repeat to the minister what has been said to me, that in the judgment of the parties who made the statement the purchase of these inferior animals was, in a large measure, a matter of straight graft, that the breeders of the inferior stock were getting an undue advantage at the hands of the Government, and that the localities in which these inferior animals were distributed were not receiving the benefit that was in contemplation by the Government in the instigation and carrying forward of this policy.
The second system of assistance that the minister has described to the House is, of course, directly in the line of encouragement of local enterprise-an enterprise, I would say, of a high class. Wherever that arrangement can be made I think it would be more beneficial, both directly and indirectly, than for the Government itself to send in the stock. I thought it was only right I should acquaint the minister with the statements that were made to me. I have no personal knowledge of the matter, but I can assure him that the statements

Were made to me by men whose opinion I could not very well gainsay, and I think it* would be well for him to make very careful inquiry in future transactions of this kind, both on account of the direct and indirect effect, namely, the failure to produce the class of stock desired, and the discouragement of local enterprise.

I am very glad to hear any suggestions from my hon. friend. I am quite sure he understands that I am cordially in sympathy with what he states to be the objects of this work. He suggests that we might be barring out local enterprise. When we established this policy it was laid down as a fundamental principle that we should not attempt to do this work in any district where we should be competing with private owners of animals. In any district where private owners bad animals available for that part of the country we did not think it was our function to send in an animal of the same type. This scheme, of assistance was primarily designed to supply those districts that had great difficulty in getting pure bred sires, and were using scrub stock. Of course, it is not possible, in distributing 3,000 animals, to get satisfaction in every individual case, the human equation being what it is in buying and selling and arranging matters of this kind. I have no doubt that mistakes have been made, but I do not think there have been many. I am quite sure I could give abundant evidence as to the general satisfactory character of the work that has been accomplished. I should be very glad, indeed, if my hon. friend and any other hon. member would bring to my attention any such opinion as he has touched upon tonight, for I think the best service that can be done to any department is to point out any weaknesses that may exist, in order that the minister may strengthen them. I have no idea at all of encouraging mistakes, or graft, or anything of that kind. I shall be only too glad to have cases of this kind brought to my attention, in order that I may have them traced up and see that they do not occur aga;n.

It was with that view
that I brought the matter to the minister's attention. Not that I wish to interfere or bring any charges, but merely that he should be on his guard against such an occurrence. I would not have it understood that I have made these remarks to discourage local enterprise or to lead in any way to the support of local enterprise against the action of the department. I was merely making a general statement that the

action .of the department must necessarily have the effect of deterring, not preventing, local enterprise.

Now that my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has mentioned it, I would remind the minister that there is always a certain amount of gossip to the effect that the department buys sites of various kinds that are not up to standard, because of political favouritism, paying big prices for them, and sends them out in different sections of the country. I do not know anything of that kind personally, so I am not making any accusation by any means; but I join with the hon. member for Edmonton in warning the minister that that would he a had thing for the department.

I frankly admit it, a
very bad thing.

I quite believe that the minister himself would not encourage anything of that kind. As to the other system of encouraging the grouping of farmers to buy really high-class horses for a neighbourhood, I think that is an excellent idea. But, so far as heavy-draught horses are concerned, in our section we do not need any encouragement of that kind, for we have as good as any the world produces in all classes of heavy horses. In former years, in our section of the country, when race horses were more generally bred there, we had a better class of saddle horses than at present. That is why I put my question with reference to the thoroughbred. I am sorry to see the thoroughbred to a great extent passing out in many sections of the country. The thoroughbred crossed with a sound mare, not too heavy a mare, produced, to my knowledge and experience, some excellent saddle horses; and it is a pity they are going out. But, I suppose, the gasolene thoroughbred does, away with them to a great extent.
The department has a representative at Sherbrooke buying thor-oughhred horses for the Government. Is it the intention of the Government to continue that system of buying horses?
We are largely dropping out of that phase of the work, for the reason I have mentioned-that we are giving more attention to encouraging farmers' associations in the use of good horses.

I have been asked by
some of our people for information which [DOT] I could not give. I have heard rumours- I do not know whether they are true or not
-that a large number of horses have been bought, many of them of inferior quality, and distributed to the farmers on certain conditions, but that the farmers did not find them profitable and consequently returned them. If my information is correct, a large number of these horses were collected and last fall sent to a lumber camp to be used all winter, and were returned in no very good condition this spring. I see by the Auditor General's report that Mr. C. N. Lester has drawn from $1,200 to $1,500 for the keep of horses. From personal knowledge I know nothing about the matter. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCrea) can understand that a very large number of animals are bought throughout the country. It will occur in the case of some associations that the animals will not be well taken care of-that occurs even in the case of private ownership, and these associations do not always live up to the spirit of their obligations. In . such cases, and where the animals are in bad condition, we gather them together and have them taken care of, and, in some cases, sell them. I do not know as to the facts of the case to which he has referred, but I shall be glad to look into it and get for him such information as I can. I can only assure him that nothing of the kind to which he refers has been encouraged by the department, nor do we want to see anything hut the best returns for the money spent.

A good deal has been said about the Government's policy of distributing thoroughbred livestock throughout the country. I do not think that anything has been done by any Department of Agriculture that has so stimulated the livestock industry as this policy adopted by the present minister. In our section the farmers have received a great benefit, and in the outlying districts particularly the livestock has been greatly improved. If you

were to go through districts to-day which you had known five years ago, you Vrould see a great improvement in the quality of the livestock. There is no doubt that in some cases, as my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) well knows, the condition of horses or other animals may be such that they will need to be taken in, so to say, for repair. I would assume that that is the reason why these horses were with Mr. C. N. Lester. With so many horses distributed to all sections of the country, there has to be some place to take these horses when they are not in a condition for breeding purposes. I would assume that that was the reason why Mr. C. N. Lester's stable was used for that purpose. We have four horses in Compton and they have all proved to be splendid successes. They are doing a great deal of good and not interfering with any private enterprises, as was suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton. They have been placed in districts where there were no other good sires of particular breeding available. Consequently as I say, they have done a great deal of good. The same would apply to other pure bred sires, bulls, rams and boars. As far as the county I represent is concerned, they have derived a great deal of benefit from this particular policy and I would favour an extension of that policy until it would attain the result of placing pure bred animals in every district in this country. The, western part of Canada needs it just as much as eastern Canada. Farmers, particularly in the newer districts', may not toe able to go out and buy pure bred sires, or, if they are able, they may neglect to do so. If they neglect it, a policy like this is bound to encourage the greatest industry that the country has-the livestock industry.

What are, briefly, the rules of the department in regard to the distribution of these animals?

The people form an association among themselves under general rules laid down, and we engage to send them any sire of any particular, breed that the majority may want. They must undertake to maintain it and keep it in proper shape.
